[{:db/id 17592186054396 :question/id #uuid "6ce1d2ce-e99a-5f5c-a698-3f744805ef24" :question/math-academy-id "e-12921" :question/problem "Calculate $(-3)^3 \div 6$." :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. First, we compute the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}\underbrace{(-3)^{3}}_{-27}÷6=(-27)÷6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-27)÷6 &= \frac{(-27)}{6} \\ &= -\frac{27}{6} \\ &= -\frac{27÷3}{6÷3} \\ &= -\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054398 :question/id #uuid "21fccd11-6107-53b8-beb0-d0c39f23bc17" :question/math-academy-id "e-12923" :question/problem "What is the value of $\left( 5 \div (-2)^2 \right) \times \left( -\dfrac{4}{5} \right).$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. First, consider the expression inside the parenthesis:

$$
\begin{aligned}5÷(-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}5÷(-2)^{2} &= 5÷4 \\ &= \frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overbrace{5÷(-2)^{2}}^{\frac{5}{4}})\times \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) &= \frac{5}{4}\times \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) \\ &= -\frac{5}{4}\times \frac{4}{5} \\ &= -\frac{5\times 4}{4\times 5} \\ &= -\frac{\cancel{5}\times \cancel{4}}{\cancel{4}\times \cancel{5}} \\ &= -1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054440 :question/id #uuid "1acb903b-bdf0-5d16-8a1c-6fdce21f4c84" :question/math-academy-id "e-13172" :question/problem "If $A = \{3, 21, 147,1\,029,\ldots,5\,931\,980\,229\},$ then what is $|A|?$" :question/worked-solution "The cardinality of a finite set $A$ is the number of elements in $A.$ 

Notice that the elements of our set 

$$
3, \quad 21, \quad 147, \quad 1\,029,\quad \ldots
$$

form a geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=7{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =7 \\  & =\frac{21}{3} \\  & =\frac{147}{21} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The $n$th term of our geometric sequence, denoted $a_n,$ is given by

$$
a_n = a_1 r^{n-1} = 3(7^{n-1}) = \dfrac37(7)^n.
$$

Therefore, we can express $A$ in set-builder notation as follows:

$$
A = \left\{\dfrac37(7)^n : n\in \mathbb N,\: 1\leq n \leq N \right\}
$$

where $N\in \mathbb N$ is to be determined.

To find $N,$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{7}(7)^{N} & =5\,931\,980\,229 \\ {7}^{N} & =13\,841\,287\,201 \\ N & ={log}_{7}⁡(13\,841\,287\,201) \\ N & =\frac{{log}_{10}⁡(13\,841\,287\,201)}{{log}_{10}⁡(7)} \\ N & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our set $A$ can be expressed as

$$
A = \left\{\dfrac37(7)^n : n\in \mathbb N,\: 1\leq n \leq 12\right\}.
$$

Finally, since $A$ has $12$ elements, we must have $|A| = 12.$"} {:db/id 17592186054526 :question/id #uuid "71af77a8-8b16-59f5-b6fb-0c344c3b9f90" :question/math-academy-id "e-3943" :question/problem "Simplify $\textrm{i}^{15}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the value of $\textrm{i}$ to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=15.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
15\div 4 = 3\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{3}.
$$

So the remainder is $\color{blue}3.$ Therefore,

$$
\textrm{i}^{15} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{3}} = -\textrm{i}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054527 :question/id #uuid "3bc3d3e9-6745-5021-b571-a301851d7bb9" :question/math-academy-id "e-3944" :question/problem "If $a = \textrm{i}^9$ and $b = \textrm{i}^{7},$ then $ab =$" :question/worked-solution "Using the addition law for exponents, we have

$$
ab =\textrm{i}^9\cdot\textrm{i}^7 = \textrm{i}^{9+7} = \textrm{i}^{16}.
$$

To find the value of $\textrm{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n,$ we divide $n$ by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=16.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
16\div 4 = 4\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{0}.
$$

So the remainder is $\color{blue}0.$ Therefore,

$$
\textrm{i}^{16} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{0}} =1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054540 :question/id #uuid "fc85eeb4-dbc0-5ea7-af3a-60270d6ae722" :question/math-academy-id "e-4089" :question/problem "Calculate $\log_{16}(32)$ without using a calculator." :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
\log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}
$$

In our case, we have $a=16$ and $X =32.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $2,$ we set $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{16}⁡(32) & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡(32)}{{log}_{2}⁡(16)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5})}{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{4})} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054541 :question/id #uuid "15844e53-9573-5e6f-8fef-debbe0a142ba" :question/math-academy-id "e-4091" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $\log x ?$ 

I. $\dfrac {\log_{2} x} {\log_{2} 10}$

II. $\dfrac {\log_{2} 10} {\log_{2} x}$

III. $\log_{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{10}\right)$" :question/worked-solution "The change of base formula for logarithms is

$$
\log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}.
$$

The change of base formula works with any new base. In this example, the choices are written using base $2,$ so we rewrite $\log x$ in terms of $\log_2.$
This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡x & ={log}_{10}⁡x \\  & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡x}{{log}_{2}⁡10}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186054543 :question/id #uuid "890afebc-d130-5dbc-aaf7-c2cd4db193f6" :question/math-academy-id "e-4100" :question/problem "Use a calculator to evaluate $\log_3 (7)$ rounded to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let's calculate $\log_3 (7)$ by changing the base $3$ to the common logarithm (base $10$).

We use the change of base formula:

$$
\log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}
$$

In our case, we have $a=3,$ $X =7,$ and $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(7) & =\frac{{log}_{10}⁡(7)}{{log}_{10}⁡(3)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(7)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\  & ≈\frac{0.845\,10}{0.477\,12} \\  & ≈1.77.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055040 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "133715ba-2604-5ba6-af84-c93f8f8812f4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186051765}] :question/id #uuid "c2594f98-66fa-5bdb-980f-e913a5a2f02c" :question/math-academy-id "q-171352" :question/problem "$6 \div 3 + (-3)^{3} =$ {{field-1}}"} {:db/id 17592186055042 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "2a175074-6bce-59a4-8bac-94c89309b66f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186051767}] :question/id #uuid "e5cf55bf-6fee-5162-aab9-57758108d29e" :question/math-academy-id "q-171356" :question/problem "$(4 \div (-2) + 5)^{4} =$ {{field-1}}"} {:db/id 17592186055074 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bd6edde5-507c-5ff6-8c58-ea2a1b440718" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186286519}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186286519} :answer-field/id #uuid "3c26fd7f-de11-54f6-a913-91718d9fcabd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186287273}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d64c45b7-2d40-58ad-9748-05e941de30d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-181454" :question/problem "If $A={3,6,12,24,48,…,98\,304},$ then $|A|=${{field-1}}." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "The cardinality of a finite set $A$ is the number of elements in $A.$ 

Notice that the elements of our set 

$$
3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,…
$$

form a geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The $n$th term of our geometric sequence, denoted ${a}_{n},$ is given by

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}=3({2}^{n-1})=\frac{3}{2}(2)^{n}.
$$

Therefore, we can express $A$ in set-builder notation as follows:

$$
A={\frac{3}{2}(2)^{n}:n\in N,\,1\le n\le N}
$$

where $N\in N$ is to be determined.

To find $N,$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}(2)^{N} & =98\,304 \\ {2}^{N} & =65\,536 \\ N & ={log}_{2}⁡(65\,536) \\ N & =\frac{{log}_{10}⁡(65\,536)}{{log}_{10}⁡(2)} \\ N & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our set $A$ can be expressed as

$$
A={\frac{3}{2}(2)^{n}:n\in N,\,1\le n\le 16}.
$$

Finally, since $A$ has $16$ elements, we must have $|A|=16.$"} {:db/id 17592186055091 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "04bef4d4-9dda-5d85-8465-cc54ae0d2df9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186051990}] :question/id #uuid "2ba1b10f-df3c-5fcf-a5e1-6e4a077ce473" :question/math-academy-id "q-184065" :question/problem "$((-4)^{2} + 5 \cdot 2) - ((-2)^{3} \div (-4)) =$ {{field-1}}"} {:db/id 17592186055183 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ca66def7-3c65-5210-99d9-f0db68c4888c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186522440} {:answer/id #uuid "745edc25-a61b-4419-a155-2f8412f950ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac32" :db/id 17592186651036}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186522440} :answer-field/id #uuid "72fdab3a-5e80-5092-81a0-756921237d3c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186052384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3ba35fd5-f0a2-573b-abd8-5bda612260aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-262884" :question/problem "Expressed as a fraction in its simplest form, ${log}_{16}⁡(64)$ equals{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=16$ and $X=64.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $2,$ we set $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{16}⁡(64) & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡(64)}{{log}_{2}⁡(16)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{6})}{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{4})} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055462 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "96517480-c58a-580a-bd6c-7724f8c25364" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186054010} {:answer/id #uuid "d6f3604e-93c4-543c-85d4-015c8fe7e1ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186054011} {:answer/id #uuid "f2d3f4da-921c-581d-b2f2-9c94396b9176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186054012} {:answer/id #uuid "1bd17a35-4d96-574e-94c2-099f33db7738" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/id 17592186054013} {:answer/id #uuid "2d69af09-12b4-5f14-a76b-d95e41ad99a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186054014}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186054014} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c9c30ac-745b-5ac6-8f1f-5c84b0f7083a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186054009}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d4f6e3a6-36a7-5dcc-b176-d20ea50c924d" :question/math-academy-id "q-66882" :question/problem "${log}_{36}⁡(\sqrt[3]{6})=$" :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=36$ and $X=\sqrt[3]{6}.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ can be presented as a power of $6,$ we set $b=6.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{36}⁡(\sqrt[3]{6}) & =\frac{{log}_{6}⁡(\sqrt[3]{6})}{{log}_{6}⁡(36)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{6}⁡({6}^{1/3})}{{log}_{6}⁡({6}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055516 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "83ff33ee-caa6-51d8-958d-bfcfda022a62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186054334} {:answer/id #uuid "ac037dd2-aa67-5dda-91e5-2a864d1cc729" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186054335} {:answer/id #uuid "c8f7a19d-57a8-550f-b117-e9656ddde586" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186054336} {:answer/id #uuid "d8bc585d-ed81-566c-b6a6-a612bcdd6c87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186054337} {:answer/id #uuid "05d90b4d-f42c-59f3-afaf-50adcb8c8df2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186054338}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186054334} :answer-field/id #uuid "15a9598e-3841-5a8c-b408-bd666ace4326" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186054333}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2013c32c-5fa6-5fa3-be49-a548908a8a84" :question/math-academy-id "q-957" :question/problem "Calculate ${log}_{9}⁡(27)$ without using a calculator." :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=9,$ and $X=27.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $3,$ we set $b=3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{9}⁡(27) & =\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(27)}{{log}_{3}⁡(9)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{3})}{{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055970 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to evaluate $\log_{4}9,$ but our calculator only has a key for the common logarithm $\log$ (base $10$).

In such cases, we can use the **change of base formula**, which states that

$$
\log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}.
$$

It effectively allows us to change a logarithm from one base, $a,$ to another, $b.$ Note that $X,$ $a,$ and $b$ have to be all greater than zero and that $a \ne 1,$ $b \ne 1.$ 

We usually choose the value of base $b$ that makes the problem easier. In particular, if we need to evaluate the expression using a calculator, we choose $b=10$ or $b=e$. 

For example, to evaluate $\log_{4}9$ using this formula, we can rewrite the logarithm from base $a=4$ to base $b=10.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡9 & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡9}{\operatorname{log}⁡4} \\  & ≈\frac{0.954\,242}{0.602\,059} \\  & =1.585\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "bb104b87-e850-5cff-9826-fdd61c0287d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2797 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186056032 :tutorial/content "A **variable** is any letter or symbol that can be replaced by a number. For example, the letters

$$
x, \quad y, \quad z, \quad a, \quad b, \quad c, \quad k, \quad m,\quad n,\quad p, \quad q,\quad r, \quad \ldots
$$

are commonly used as variables. But in general, we can use any letter we like.

An **algebraic expression** is a combination of variables with mathematical operations, like addition $(+)$, subtraction $(-)$, multiplication $(\times)$, and division $(\div).$ So 

$$
x+2,\qquad 6-y,\qquad 2\times p + 1,\qquad q\div r,
$$

are all examples of algebraic expressions." :tutorial/id #uuid "232cd5fe-049f-512d-8d7c-ad600a7e6a81" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8165 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186056074 :tutorial/content "Before we continue, we need a brief discussion on the concept of **integer divisibility.**

Suppose $a$ and $b$ are integers. We write $a  \mid b$ to mean that $\boldsymbol a$ **divides** $\boldsymbol b.$ Informally, this means the quotient of $\dfrac b a$ is an *integer*, and there is *no remainder*. 

For example, consider the following statement:

$$
5 \,|\, 20
$$

This statement reads, "$5$ divides $20$". Moreover, this is a *true* statement because $20\div 5 = 4$ is an integer. 

Now consider the following statement:

$$
6\,  |\, 20
$$

This statement is *false* because $20\div 6 = 3 {\color{blue}{\dfrac13}},$ which is *not* an integer. The correct statement is

$$
6 \! \not | \: 20.
$$

This statement reads, "$6$ does not divide $20$".

For now, this is all we need to understand the notation $a\mid b.$ More formal discussions on integer divisibility will be given in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "ac10b43c-74e8-5752-9d06-2d746c31cb0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9348 :tutorial/title "Divisibility Notation"} {:db/id 17592186059432 :question/id #uuid "eaf86423-5f7e-5da2-aa3d-cf35e9b16b13" :question/math-academy-id "e-13308" :question/problem "Let $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that if $2a \equiv 2b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 14)$, then $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 7)$." :question/worked-solution "We start by using the definition of modular congruence. Recall that

$$
a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad n \mid (a-b) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad a-b = nk
$$

for some integer $k$.

In this case, we need to show the following:

$$
2a \equiv 2b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 14) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 7)
$$

So, we can reason as follows:

> By the definition of modular congruence,
> $2a≡2b(mod14) \mid ⇔14∣(2a - 2b); ⇔14∣2(a - b)$

Next, we use the definition of divisibility:

> By the definition of divisibility in $\mathbb{Z}$, $14 \mid 2(a-b)$ means that there exists an integer $k$ such that
> $2(a-b) = 14k$.

Now, we can cancel out the factor of $2{:}$

> Dividing this equation by $2$, we obtain
> $a-b = 7k$,
> which in turn implies
> $7 \mid (a-b)$.

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence again:

> Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have
> $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 7)$."} {:db/id 17592186059439 :question/id #uuid "7c0d4a9d-2451-5571-a428-13532b1adbf2" :question/math-academy-id "e-13419" :question/problem "What is the value of $8 \,\dfrac{7}{9} - 4 \,\dfrac{4}{9} \,$?" :question/worked-solution "To subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, we subtract

- whole numbers from whole numbers, and
- fractions from fractions.

With that in mind, let's subtract our mixed numbers.

- Subtracting the whole numbers, we get
$8 - 4 = {\color{red}{4}}$.
- Subtracting the fractions, we get
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{7}{9} - \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{7 - 4}{9} = \dfrac{3}{9}.
$$
We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $3{:}$
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{3 \div 3}{9 \div 3} = {\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{3}}}
$$

Finally, we combine the resulting whole number and fraction to create a mixed number:

$$
8 \,\dfrac{7}{9} - 4 \,\dfrac{4}{9} = {\color{red}{4}}\,{\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{3}}}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059453 :question/id #uuid "d7516cec-bd96-59db-98cd-5d82e41fa719" :question/math-academy-id "e-14763" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $A$ given below?

- $\det(A) = 0$

- $A$ is **not** a singular matrix

- $A$ is a singular matrix

$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 7\end{array} \right]}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 7\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 4 & 7\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 7\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-4)-2(7-3)+3(4-0) \\  & =-4-2\cdot 4+3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4-8+12 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements I and III are true."} {:db/id 17592186059469 :question/id #uuid "762e323d-62be-5cd0-ad06-7b11af56fe3f" :question/math-academy-id "e-3136" :question/problem "Simplify the trigonometric expression $\sin^4{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor $\sin^2\theta$ from the expression:

$$
\sin^4{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta} = \sin^2{\theta}\cdot(\sin^2{\theta}+\cos^2{\theta})
$$

Then, we use $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}) & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\sin^4{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta} = \sin^2\theta.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059470 :question/id #uuid "f2b7e482-2bcd-5bd2-91ee-66415b375da4" :question/math-academy-id "e-3137" :question/problem "Simplify the trigonometric expression $\dfrac {\cos \theta \sin^2 \theta + \cos^3 \theta}{\sin\theta}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the numerator:

$$
\dfrac {\cos \theta \sin^2 \theta + \cos^3 \theta} {\sin \theta}	=	\dfrac {\cos \theta \cdot (\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta)} {\sin \theta}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\dfrac {\cos \theta \sin^2 \theta + \cos^3 \theta} {\sin \theta} = \cot \theta.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059471 :question/id #uuid "9ee1e04e-8a36-5597-8928-c2ebd67c1b1a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3139" :question/problem "Simplify the trigonometric expression $\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\cot{\theta}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the second term using the identity $\cot \theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\dfrac{\cos{\theta}}{\sin{\theta}}
$$

Next, we put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} &= \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} &= \frac{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} \\ &= \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )} \\ &= \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ &= \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{1+\cos{\theta}}+\cot{\theta} = \csc\theta.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059475 :question/id #uuid "a218df38-fa61-5ffd-b1bd-77422b946d4c" :question/math-academy-id "e-3149" :question/problem "Simplify the trigonometric expression
$\dfrac {\cot \theta + \csc \theta} {\cos \theta + 1}$." :question/worked-solution "First, let's interpret the fraction as a division:

$$
\dfrac {\cot \theta + \csc \theta} {\cos \theta + 1} = \left(\cot \theta + \csc \theta\right)\div \left(\cos \theta + 1\right)
$$

Then, we recall the identities

$$
\cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}
$$

and

$$
\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}
$$

and we substitute them into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\cot θ + \csc θ) \div (\cos θ + 1) &= (\frac{\cos θ}{\sin θ} + \frac{1}{\sin θ}) \div (\cos θ + 1) \\
&= \left(\frac{\cos θ + 1}{\sin θ}\right) \div (\cos θ + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we turn the division into multiplication, and simplify the expression as much as possible:

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle ( {\displaystyle \frac{\cos   \theta  + 1}{\sin   \theta }} ) \div  ( \cos   \theta  + 1 ) & \displaystyle  = ( {\displaystyle \frac{\cos   \theta  + 1}{\sin   \theta }} ) \cdot  ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{\cos   \theta  + 1}} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\cos   \theta  + 1}{\sin   \theta  ( \cos   \theta  + 1 )}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{( \cos   \theta  + 1 )}}{\sin   \theta  \cancel{( \cos   \theta  + 1 )}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sin   \theta }} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \csc   \theta \end{array}}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059479 :question/id #uuid "3b9c93fe-82ac-58c5-b14a-9bcd30b1f0e9" :question/math-academy-id "e-3175" :question/problem "Simplify the trigonometric expression $\dfrac{\cos{x}}{1-\cos^2{x}}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the denominator using $1-\cos^2 x = \sin^2 x.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac{\cos{x}}{1-\cos^2{x}} = \dfrac{\cos{x}}{\sin^2{x}}.
$$

Next, we simplify the expression by separating out the factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot 1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{\cos{x}}{1-\cos^2{x}}=\cot{x}\csc{x}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059480 :question/id #uuid "e5821060-9f69-5df5-9456-a4574e92e910" :question/math-academy-id "e-3176" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $\dfrac{\cos^2 x}{1-\sin x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the numerator using $1-\sin^2 x = \cos^2 x,$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\cos^2 x}{1-\sin x} = \dfrac{1-\sin^2 x}{1-\sin x}
$$

Then, we factor the numerator as a difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x} & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\cancel{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1} \\  & =1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{\cos^2 x}{1-\sin x} = 1 + \sin x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059486 :question/id #uuid "d917e025-59a4-5df5-b412-4eb6f2c4afc7" :question/math-academy-id "e-3329" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $\sin x(2\cos x - \sin x) - \cos^2x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group the $\sin^2 x$ and $\cos^2 x$ terms. 

$$
2\sin x\cos x -(\sin^2x + \cos^2 x)
$$

Then, we use $\sin^2{x} + \cos^2{x} = 1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
2\sin x\cos x - 1
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\sin x(2\cos x - \sin x) - \cos^2x = 2\sin x\cos x - 1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059487 :question/id #uuid "056204bc-53b9-5a32-a53c-0f728729fd9f" :question/math-academy-id "e-3332" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $3\cos^2 x \left(\sec^2 x -1\right).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we expand the parentheses and simplify the resulting expression:

$$
3\cos^2 x \left(\sec^2 x -1\right) = 3\cos^2 x \sec^2 x - 3\cos^2 x
$$

Then, we use the identity $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ to further simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{cos}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-3{cos}^{2}⁡x & =3{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\right)}^{2}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{3{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{3\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡x}}{\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡x}}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3-3{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the identity $\sin^2 x = 1-\cos^2 x$ to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, as follows:

$$
3(1-\cos^2 x) = 3\cdot \sin^2 x = 3\sin^2 x
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
3\cos^2 x \left(\sec^2 x -1\right)= 3\sin^2 x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059503 :question/id #uuid "31b9e2d8-1458-50b3-a920-703476825420" :question/math-academy-id "e-3631" :question/problem "Find the derivative of $y =  3\cos x  + 4\sin x + 2x^3.$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \sin x ) = \cos x,$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \cos x ) = -\sin x.$ Applying these formulas, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3cos⁡x+4sin⁡x+2{x}^{3}) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(cos⁡x)+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(sin⁡x)+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}) \\  & =-3sin⁡x+4cos⁡x+2(3){x}^{2} \\  & =-3sin⁡x+4cos⁡x+6{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059504 :question/id #uuid "ae922c00-2ff5-5a46-805a-62955bc5a08a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3632" :question/problem "Find the slope of $y = 4\tan x + 5x$ at $x = 0.$" :question/worked-solution "The slope at $x=0$ is given by the value of the derivative $y'$ at $x=0.$ 

First, we compute the derivative, using the fact that $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (\tan x) = \sec^2 x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4tan⁡x+5x) \\  & =4{sec}^{2}⁡x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =4{sec}^{2}⁡0+5 \\  & =4\cdot 1+5 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope is $9.$"} {:db/id 17592186059509 :question/id #uuid "0a0ef460-7a16-5dc9-b522-567f0462c678" :question/math-academy-id "e-3771" :question/problem "$1 - \cos \left(\dfrac \pi 2 - y \right) \sin y=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the cofunction identity for sine and cosine:

$$
\cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y \right) = \sin y
$$

Substituting this into our expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 - \cos(\frac{π}{2} - y)\sin y &= 1 - \siny\sin y \\
&= 1 - \sin^{2} y \\
&= \cos^{2} y
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059518 :question/id #uuid "3590f0e0-2ff9-58f4-8351-772b477c1cd2" :question/math-academy-id "e-4109" :question/problem "If $\log_7 (2x + 1) = 1,$ then what is $x?$" :question/worked-solution "To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(2x+1) & =1 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(2x+1)} & ={7}^{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $7^{\log_7 (2x + 1)} = 2x+1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & =7 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059557 :question/id #uuid "2b6e8845-a53d-510c-b44f-1b00271ee507" :question/math-academy-id "e-4434" :question/problem "Calculate $\det(A),$ if <div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>" :question/worked-solution "For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot 6-2\cdot 5 \\  & =18-10 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059558 :question/id #uuid "b066b73a-c777-550c-9c6e-af8093bf7fab" :question/math-academy-id "e-4435" :question/problem "Calculate $\det(A),$ if <div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$A=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & -2 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>" :question/worked-solution "For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{2} & -2 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{3}-(-2)\cdot 0 \\  & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059559 :question/id #uuid "043a5e58-e1a0-50a5-b1be-d404e6262991" :question/math-academy-id "e-4436" :question/problem "If
$$
\displaystyle {A} = 
    \left\lbrack
    \begin{matrix}
        2 & -1  \\
        -3 & k
    \end{matrix}
    \right\rbrack
$$
and
$\det({A}) = 5$, what is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & k\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot k-(-1)\cdot (-3) \\  & =2k-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A)=5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =5 \\ 2k-3 & =5 \\ 2k & =8 \\ k & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059560 :question/id #uuid "79841c0d-e191-566b-8fe2-63828dcfc23a" :question/math-academy-id "e-4439" :question/problem "Calculate the minor of the entry $b_{21}$ in the matrix
$$
B= 
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}10 & 1 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 & 8 \\ 4 & 7 & 2\end{array} \right]}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The minor of $b_{21} = 3$ (second row, first column) is the determinant of the remaining entries when the column and row containing $3$ are removed: 

$$
B= 
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{gray}∗} & 1 & 5 \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{ {\color{gray}3}} & {\color{gray}∗} & {\color{gray}∗} \\ {\color{gray}∗} & 7 & 2\end{array} \right]}
$$

So, the minor of $b_{21}=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 2-5\cdot 7 \\  & =2-35 \\  & =-33.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059561 :question/id #uuid "51f60726-3d12-507e-b942-5d316fc28bd0" :question/math-academy-id "e-4440" :question/problem "What is the minor of $c_{22}$ in the matrix
$$
C=
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}7 x & 0 & - 3 y \\ 1 & x + 2 y & 4 \\ - y & 0 & 5\end{array} \right]}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we remove the second row and second column: 

$$
C=
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}7 x & {\color{gray}∗} & - 3 y \\ {\color{gray}∗} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{ {\color{gray}x + 2 y}} & {\color{gray}∗} \\ - y & {\color{gray}∗} & 5\end{array} \right]}
$$

Next, we calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}7x & -3y \\ -y & 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}7x & -3y \\ -y & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =7x\cdot 5-(-3y)\cdot (-y) \\  & =35x-3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059562 :question/id #uuid "afd06762-0a78-5559-b035-98bd05e6c084" :question/math-academy-id "e-4441" :question/problem "Given that the minor of $a_{23}$ is $5,$ find all the possible values of $k$ in the matrix
$$
A= {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}k & 3 & - 1 \\ - 5 & 2 & 7 \\ - 1 & 2 k & - 6\end{array} \right]}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we remove the second row and third column:

$$
A= {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}k & 3 & {\color{gray}∗} \\ {\color{gray}∗} & {\color{gray}∗} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{ {\color{gray}7}} \\ - 1 & 2 k & {\color{gray}∗}\end{array} \right]}
$$

The minor of $a_{23}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}k & 3 \\ -1 & 2k\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}k & 3 \\ -1 & 2k\end{vmatrix} \\  & =k\cdot 2k-3\cdot (-1) \\  & =2{k}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the minor of $a_{23}$ is $5,$ so we must have:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{k}^{2}+3 & =5 \\ 2{k}^{2} & =2 \\ {k}^{2} & =1 \\ k & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $k=-1$ and $k=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186059563 :question/id #uuid "8cd94856-fbe5-53a4-b7f2-f5b29b7aa927" :question/math-academy-id "e-4514" :question/problem "Find the inverse of $A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 4 & - 3 & 8\end{array} \right]}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 4 & -3 & 8\end{vmatrix} & =0\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 8\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 8\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-(8-12)+2(-3-0) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 8\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 8\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 8\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 8\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 4 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -4 & -3 \\ 14 & -8 & -4 \\ 3 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}9 & - ( - 4 ) & - 3 \\ - ( 14 ) & - 8 & - ( - 4 ) \\ 3 & - ( - 2 ) & - 1\end{array} \right]}
={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}9 & 4 & - 3 \\ - 14 & - 8 & 4 \\ 3 & 2 & - 1\end{array} \right]}
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
C^{T}={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}9 & - 14 & 3 \\ 4 & - 8 & 2 \\ - 3 & 4 & - 1\end{array} \right]}
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -14 & 3 \\ 4 & -8 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -14 & 3 \\ 4 & -8 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{9}{2} & 7 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & -1 \\ \frac{3}{2} & -2 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059564 :question/id #uuid "9180ff3b-46d2-5df7-81b6-ac75bef51e00" :question/math-academy-id "e-4515" :question/problem "The entry $a'_{31}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}3 & 2 & - 2 \\ - 2 & k & 0 \\ - 1 & - 3 & 3\end{array} \right]}
$$ 
equals $1$. Find the value of $k$." :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & k & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 3\end{vmatrix} & =3\begin{vmatrix}k & 0 \\ -3 & 3\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(3k-0)-2(-6-0)-2(6+k) \\  & =9k+12-12-2k \\  & =7k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry $a'_{31}$ in $A^{-1},$ we need to know the value of $c_{13}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{13} & =(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =6+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det (A)}C^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13} \\  & =\frac{1}{7k}\cdot (6+k) \\  & =\frac{6+k}{7k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that $a'_{31}=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6+k}{7k} & =1 \\ 6+k & =7k \\ 6 & =6k \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059565 :question/id #uuid "26e9a55f-7711-5d8f-ab0a-e8638f2d2dec" :question/math-academy-id "e-4516" :question/problem "Determine the entry $a'_{23}$ in the inverse of the matrix $A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}- 2 & 3 & - 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & - 1 & 2\end{array} \right]}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}+(-3)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2(2-0)-3(0-0)-3(0-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry $a'_{23}$ in $A^{-1},$ we need to know the value of $c_{32}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{32} & =(-1)^{3+2}{M}_{32} \\  & =(-1)^{5}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1\cdot (0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det (A)}C^{T},$ we have

$$
a'_{23} = \dfrac{1}{-1}c_{32} = -1\cdot 0 = 0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059592 :question/id #uuid "7055ec96-b829-5cca-8149-314b4c8fc6c8" :question/math-academy-id "e-5111" :question/problem "Given that $2\log_5 (x-3)+1 = 5,$ then what is the value of $x?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make $\log_5 (x-3)$ the subject of the equation by moving everything else to the right-hand side. This gives

$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $5,$ so we use a base of $5$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =2 \\ {5}^{{log}_{5}⁡(x-3)} & ={5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $5^{\log_5 (x - 3)} = x-3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & ={5}^{2} \\ x-3 & =25 \\ x & =28\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059593 :question/id #uuid "77f6d553-3291-5110-a30e-11991ae88425" :question/math-academy-id "e-5118" :question/problem "If $\log_2 x = 5,$ then what is the value of $x?$" :question/worked-solution "To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. :question/id #uuid "d0d9bc49-c94e-5174-9068-2abf75c42684" :question/math-academy-id "q-128490" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $M$ given below?

$$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{5} & 0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \\ -3\sqrt{5} & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -3\sqrt{5} & 4\end{vmatrix}+\frac{1}{3}\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3\sqrt{5} & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\sqrt{5}(12-15)-0+\frac{1}{3}(0+9\sqrt{5}) \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot (-3)+\frac{1}{3}\cdot 9\sqrt{5} \\  & =-3\sqrt{5}+3\sqrt{5} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(M)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statement “$M$ is a singular matrix” is true."} {:db/id 17592186060153 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f06230e-8816-51ce-b392-2abd455f3b69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186285208} {:answer/id #uuid "4e8539bc-f4a1-50db-90f6-0b45e3ceff04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186285517} {:answer/id #uuid "52f9a129-aa6f-59fe-9748-78c62d9d1a3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186285550} {:answer/id #uuid "d79adfbb-4209-5e76-80b7-c3a2f369dbcc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{20}" :db/id 17592186286751} {:answer/id #uuid "f6b8e647-e565-5c04-9e76-013451742246" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186287048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186285517} :answer-field/id #uuid "cec0d804-b8fa-5b33-8525-d5694c64c34d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186287572}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ce77ea41-d1eb-55f8-914d-e1a94a42a6b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-18279" :question/problem "Determine the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}-(-2)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}+4\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0)+2(0+1)+4(0+3) \\  & =6+2+12 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-4-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we expand the parenthesis and use the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right))}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)+{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right) \\  & =[{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)+{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)]-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right) \\  & =1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{12}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right) & =1-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right))}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060347 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23fa492c-2b6f-575d-887c-9228be9a16f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186333322} {:answer/id #uuid "8d7c6404-2b25-54fa-94d0-6f77d064763b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186334251} {:answer/id #uuid "95cc9a2a-f119-5a30-83a9-1de8f468d8a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186334323} {:answer/id #uuid "b1d83c2b-3dc3-52bb-b1dd-c662d588dbae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{sin}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186334549} {:answer/id #uuid "dd5708a4-4e83-57c4-b5c5-e5fe68d5f4dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186334922}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186334251} :answer-field/id #uuid "b36ee6a4-c232-5bf3-bd7c-ec897ad3be2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335567}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c024ed7c-9654-5da5-b602-2f368dd77de2" :question/math-academy-id "q-65181" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the numerator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x.$

$$

equals $18.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ k & 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ k & 0\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ k & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-24)-2(0-4k)+3(0-k) \\  & =8k-3k-24 \\  & =5k-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(0-18) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{5k-24}\cdot 18 \\  & =\frac{18}{5k-24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{13}^{′}=18$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{5k-24} & =18 \\ \frac{1}{5k-24} & =1 \\ 1 & =5k-24 \\ 25 & =5k \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060454 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "141d3bda-708e-5cd1-a9c3-33813075f0e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438670} {:answer/id #uuid "c97bfd73-22d0-514a-b96a-af8b07567307" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438671}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438671} :answer-field/id #uuid "e441ef7a-f7d8-556c-897f-7d0c7a6b2bc1" :answer-field/key "$det(F)=0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439364} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa853019-8cb7-57bb-8d89-07bb087c8654" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438672} {:answer/id #uuid "5e56b566-9992-53f1-aacf-331d0f084061" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438673}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438673} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6cc4081-efb3-5cbd-91d9-77bb4d9690f4" :answer-field/key "$F$ is a singular matrix" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439365} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1db0c840-997f-55b7-bab1-3572f80549a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438674} {:answer/id #uuid "9da77c68-30c2-574d-8a12-c8183bf926de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438675}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438674} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e1cd461-5747-5d77-9466-83683a668421" :answer-field/key "$det(F)=-2$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439366}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c4279505-241a-54e3-b9b3-ff9b46d09cfd" :question/math-academy-id "q-9838" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $F$ given below?

Select all that apply.

$$
F=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 & 8\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(F) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 7 & 8\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 6 & 8\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1(24-30)+2(21-24) \\  & =0-1\cdot (-6)+2\cdot (-3) \\  & =6-6 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(F)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements $det(F)=0$ and “$F$ is a singular matrix” are true."} {:db/id 17592186060458 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2e2a7fa-1a07-507e-9cfb-d555fed4d92f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 5 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186059371} {:answer/id #uuid "413612e5-67ec-5bfe-a7b4-1ae63f30a529" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -7 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186059372} {:answer/id #uuid "4c1f7f26-d02f-5e3f-a75e-088281efd141" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186059373} {:answer/id #uuid "4f81fba0-53c1-5618-97a3-e5a601c25bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186059374} {:answer/id #uuid "4fa3e0c4-2a51-5f34-aca2-36798ca2ba7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186059375}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186059375} :answer-field/id #uuid "0e2f5d0b-4478-5dc8-803a-bd9eeb731d12" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186059370}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "86bd8759-9672-5297-874b-c9bf15a86252" :question/math-academy-id "q-9965" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
given that $det(A) = 5$." :question/worked-solution "Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** Find the determinant of $A$.

$$
\det(A)=(1)(5)+(-1)(-6)+(3)(-2)=5.
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of minors. Delete row $i$ and column $j$ to obtain $M_{ij}$. For example,

$$
M_{11}=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}=5.
$$

Computing the remaining minors gives

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & 7 & -4 \\ -5 & -4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3:** Apply the alternating signs $(-1)^{i+j}$ to form the cofactor matrix.

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -6 & -2 \\ -5 & 7 & 4 \\ -5 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 4:** Transpose the matrix of cofactors.

$$
C^T=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 5:** Divide by the nonzero determinant.

$$
A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}C^T=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ - \frac{6}{5} & \frac{7}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ - \frac{2}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060459 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9e65ae8a-57ce-5eb7-8254-bbe131d8f40c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186059377} {:answer/id #uuid "b31705b8-2e69-5452-b12a-9cd85d22b26a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186059378} {:answer/id #uuid "ff8b60ca-2038-56d9-bf33-2d7df3d1d28d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186059379} {:answer/id #uuid "1c2241db-dca5-5b98-b283-c76148dd792e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186059380} {:answer/id #uuid "58134502-f6c0-5d83-9274-d6f7f28fca66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186059381}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186059377} :answer-field/id #uuid "168f3dd3-003b-54d0-ae3c-e643ac553095" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186059376}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c04effc9-bb43-5aa7-be8b-3e036c90cdc8" :question/math-academy-id "q-9997" :question/problem "The entry $a_{23}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$$
\displaystyle A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & k & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$
equals $-1$ and $det(A) = 4 - 4k$. Find the value of $k$." :question/worked-solution "Since $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det(A)}C^T,$ the entry $a_{23}^{\prime}$ uses the cofactor $C_{32}$. Remove row $3$ and column $2$ to get

$$
C_{32}=(-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}=-4.
$$

Using the given determinant, we obtain

$$
a_{23}^{\prime}=\frac{-4}{4-4k}.
$$

The inverse exists only when $k\ne1$. Set this entry equal to $-1$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-4}{4-4k}&=-1\\-4&=-4+4k\\k&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

At $k=0,$ the determinant is $4\ne0,$ so this value is valid."} {:db/id 17592186060863 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the law of cosines in the following form:

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b,$ and $c,$ as shown below. 

![](images/7c/7cc2a0cbb6a02af829e070fc54cfdbe616683f86527b119a530053a34048e699.png)

Let's now add the height $\overline{CH}$ and assume it has length $h,$ as shown.

![](images/d4/d4e80b2b54283ea353b687d959e9d8fc6c9303e85081c0a46b48703ee3dae7d5.png)

The remainder of this proof consists of two steps:

- **Step 1**: Write down expressions for $\cos A$ and $\sin A.$

- **Step 2**: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC,$ and simplify.

Using elementary trigonometry, we have

$$
\cos A = \dfrac{AH}{b}, \qquad \sin A = \dfrac{h}{b},
$$

which can be written as

$$
AH =  b\cos A, \qquad h = b\sin A.
$$

Applying the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC$ and using our expression for $h,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{h}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the length of the side $\overline{AB}.$ Since $\overline{AB}$ consists of two segments, $\overline{AH}$ and $\overline{BH},$ we have

$$
c = AH + BH\quad \Longrightarrow\quad BH = c - AH,
$$

and using our expression for $AH,$ we have

$$
BH = c - b\cos A.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $a^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & =(c-b\operatorname{cos}⁡A)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & ={c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A+{b}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡A+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & ={b}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡A+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\  & ={b}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡A+{sin}^{2}⁡A)+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A.\end{aligned}
$$

It can be shown that $\cos^2A + \sin^2 A = 1$ for any angle $A$ (this is the Pythagorean theorem in trigonometric form). Therefore, we have

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

as required.

We can use a similar argument to prove the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{2} &={a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2ac\operatorname{cos}⁡B \\ {c}^{2} &={a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-2ab\operatorname{cos}⁡C\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6ee27fb2-d873-53a9-b674-446b546b19ec" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13281 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Law of Cosines"} {:db/id 17592186060906 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the equation $\log_3 x = 4.$ Can we determine $x?$

Recall that the inverse operation of the logarithm is exponentiation. So, to isolate $x,$ we must exponentiate both sides of this equation. 

The base of the logarithm is $3,$ so we use a base of $3$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡x & =4 \\ {3}^{({log}_{3}⁡x)} & ={3}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above may look complicated, but since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $3^{(\log_3{x})}=x.$ Therefore, we get   

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={3}^{4} \\ x & =81.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x = 81$ is the solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "bbfe9e19-d1ed-5df9-97f9-0e9c7f9f50e9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2810 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186060995 :tutorial/content "Recall the following division properties of modular arithmetic for

$$
k\neq 0{:}
$$

- The first division property states that
$ka \equiv kb \quad(\text{mod}\,kn) \quad \Rightarrow \quad a \equiv b \quad(\textrm{mod}\,n)$.

- The second division property states that
$\left(ka\equiv kb\:(\textrm{mod} \,n)\right) \:\land\: \left(\textrm{gcd}(k,n)=1\right) \quad \Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \quad(\textrm{mod}\, n)$.

Let's prove that the second property holds in the following case:

$$
\underbrace{3a \equiv 3b}_{P(a,b)} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{a \equiv b}_{Q(a,b)} \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 4)
$$

We begin our proof by assuming $P$ is true.

> *Assume* $3a \equiv 3b\:(\textrm{mod} \: 4)$.
> *Then, by the definition of modular congruence, we have*
> $3a≡3b(mod4) \mid ⇔4∣(3a - 3b); ⇔4∣3(a - b)$.

Now, we recall the following divisibility property of integers:

$$
(c \mid ab) \:\land\: (\textrm{gcd}(a,c)=1) \quad\Rightarrow\quad (c \mid b)
$$

Using this fact, we have the following:

> *Now, since $3(a-b)$ is divisible by $4$ and $\textrm{gcd}(4,3)=1$, the difference $(a-b)$ must be divisible by $4$, i.e.,*
> $4 \mid (a-b)$.

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence one more:

> *Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have*
> $a \equiv b \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 4)$.

And we're done.

Let's restate the full proof." :tutorial/id #uuid "8fd2037f-aec8-565a-9c0c-22615e446a93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8326 :tutorial/title "The Division Properties"} {:db/id 17592186061013 :tutorial/content "Proposition:

$$

$$

Proof:

> *Now, since $3(a-b)$ is divisible by $4$ and $\textrm{gcd}(4,3)=1$, the difference $(a-b)$ must be divisible by $4$, i.e.,*

"5b4f3b5f-2f0b-5178-9055-cf83a9885920" :question/math-academy-id "e-12972" :question/problem "Find the value of $-15 \div 3.$" :question/worked-solution "Here, we are dividing a negative number $\color{red}(-15)$ by a positive one $\color{blue}(3).$ So the result will be negative:
$$
{\color{red}(-15)} \div {\color{blue}3} = {\color{red}\mathbf{-} \boxed{ {\phantom{5}}} }
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $15$ by $3$ without any signs: $15 \div 3 = 5.$ Therefore, we get

$$
{\color{red}(-15)} \div {\color{blue}3} = {\color{red}-5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186063942 :question/id #uuid "166aaac7-bc88-577a-8e84-47347408e3c9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12973" :question/problem "Calculate the value of $50 \div (-5).$" :question/worked-solution "We have to divide a positive number $\color{blue}(50)$ by a negative one $\color{red}(-5).$ So the result will be negative:
$$
{\color{blue}{50}} \div {\color{red}{(-5)}} = {\color{red}{\mathbf{-} \boxed{ {\phantom{10}}} }}
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $50$ by $5$ without any signs: $50 \div 5 = 10.$ Therefore,  we get

$$
{\color{blue}{50}} \div {\color{red}{(-5)}} = {\color{red}{-10}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186063943 :question/id #uuid "e2005c9d-c0ff-5b8e-bc64-4e222fd19fdf" :question/math-academy-id "e-12976" :question/problem "Calculate $-81\div (-9).$" :question/worked-solution "We have to divide a negative number ${\color{red}(-81)}$ by another negative number ${\color{red}(-9)}.$ So the result will be positive:
$$
{\color{red}(-81)} \div {\color{red}(-9)} = {\color{blue} \boxed{ {\phantom{9}}} }
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $81$ by $9$ without any signs: $81 \div 9 = 9.$ Therefore,  we get

$$
{\color{red}(-81)} \div {\color{red}(-9)} = {\color{blue}9}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186063949 :question/id #uuid "87974d27-c494-5b1a-84e9-03e39f3e0b1c" :question/math-academy-id "e-13086" :question/problem "Calculate $\dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can use either of the following two methods.

**Method 1 - The Long Way** 

First, remember that a fraction represents a division:

$$
\dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6} = \left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)  \div 6
$$

Now, recall that dividing by $6$ is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{6}.$ We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)÷6 &= \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\times \left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ &= -\frac{3\times 1}{2\times 6} \\ &= -\frac{3}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify:

$$
- \dfrac{3}{12}  = - \dfrac{3 \div 3}{12 \div 3}  = -\dfrac{1}{4}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6}= -\dfrac14
$$

 

**Method 2 - The Quick Way**

The result will have the same numerator as the top fraction, and the denominator is just the product of the two denominators: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{6} &= \frac{-3}{2\times 6} \\ &= -\frac{3}{12} \\ &= -\frac{3÷3}{12÷3} \\ &= -\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064034 :question/id #uuid "b411bf9f-f944-505d-94dc-13df743545dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-259" :question/problem "The function $h(x)$ is given by
$$
h(x)=
{\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{\log }_{3}  ( x + c ) , & x \ne  0 , \\ 2 , & x = 0.\end{array} \right. }
$$

Given that $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=0,$ what is the value of $c?$" :question/worked-solution "From the definition of $h(x),$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}h(x) & =\lim_{x\to 0}{log}_{3}⁡(x+c) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(0+c) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(c).\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $h(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}h(x) & =h(0) \\ {log}_{3}⁡(c) & =2 \\ c & ={3}^{2} \\ c & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $c=9$ removes the point discontinuity."} {:db/id 17592186064052 :question/id #uuid "a9671d61-6b85-5d84-b49c-a6443569f6c0" :question/math-academy-id "e-382" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int 3\sin{x}\,\textrm d x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\int \sin x \, \textrm dx = -\cos x + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3sin⁡x\,\text{d}x & =3\int sin⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3(-cos⁡x)+C \\  & =-3cos⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064053 :question/id #uuid "4c3342aa-dd1c-566b-9229-164e594c554c" :question/math-academy-id "e-383" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int (-\csc x\cot x)\,\textrm d x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = - \csc x + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-csc⁡xcot⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =-\int (csc⁡xcot⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(-csc⁡x)+C \\  & =csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064055 :question/id #uuid "c2c57145-3988-5ce8-b13f-114bba6964f7" :question/math-academy-id "e-385" :question/problem "Calculate the integral $$
\displaystyle{\int} \csc{x}(\csc{x}+3\cot{x} )\, \textrm{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
\int \csc^2 x \, \textrm dx = -\cot x + C
$$

and

$$
\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = -\csc x + C.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int csc⁡x(csc⁡x+3cot⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x+3csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+3\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-cot⁡x-3csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064059 :question/id #uuid "81e3df9e-e5ab-57ec-9a82-149a277e94f0" :question/math-academy-id "e-3890" :question/problem "If $f'(x) = \dfrac{5}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}} - 2x,$ then $f(x)=$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}} \, \textrm dx = \textrm{arcsec} \, x.
$$

Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}-2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\text{arcsec}\,(x)-2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =5\text{arcsec}\,(x)-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064087 :question/id #uuid "897fedd3-db36-5614-886c-c88fba708692" :question/math-academy-id "e-4637" :question/problem "Calculate the value of $0 \div 5$." :question/worked-solution "Zero divided by any number (other than zero) equals zero. Therefore,

$$
0 \div 5 = 0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064088 :question/id #uuid "800d4367-20e6-55a9-8469-7c3654d512a0" :question/math-academy-id "e-4638" :question/problem "Compute the value of $0 \div \left(-\dfrac 1 2\right)$." :question/worked-solution "Zero divided by any number (other than zero) equals zero. Therefore,

$$
0 \div \left(-\dfrac 1 2\right) = 0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064089 :question/id #uuid "c2eb29fb-9a40-5db8-b377-14c50b87fd86" :question/math-academy-id "e-4639" :question/problem "What is $-2 \div 0$?" :question/worked-solution "We cannot divide any number by zero. Therefore, $-2 \div 0$ is undefined."} {:db/id 17592186064093 :question/id #uuid "15473603-5bb5-5a20-8fc9-e4d7589ccb38" :question/math-academy-id "e-473" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\left(\cot x + \sin^2 x\right)\,\textrm d x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x } = \csc x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064094 :question/id #uuid "68d2eb66-87ab-5182-9669-376bd1f70673" :question/math-academy-id "e-474" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x =  \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x}  = \tan x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x$ to express this as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,
$$

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064101 :question/id #uuid "56860611-869d-5035-bf8f-f568c774d78d" :question/math-academy-id "e-5014" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle {\displaystyle \int \dfrac{5\, \textrm{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^2-1}}  = }
$$" :question/worked-solution "This resembles the basic integral for $\textrm{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

Let $u = 5x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
5\,\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\,\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(5x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064127 :question/id #uuid "373a63fc-3dae-5880-8a49-63b5c64888f3" :question/math-academy-id "e-734" :question/problem "Given that $f(x) = \sin^3{x}$, calculate $f'(x).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write

$$
f(x) = (\sin{x})^3.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f = u^3, \qquad u=\sin x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 3u^2, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{x}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =3(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064128 :question/id #uuid "ceddd310-5fe4-5b55-8210-991ff22c66b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-7349" :question/problem "Peter is standing on the bank of a river. He observes a speed boat $B$ going downstream at a constant distance of $10\,\textrm{m}$ from the bank. If the boat moves at a constant speed of $8 \, \textrm{m/s}$ parallel to the bank, at what rate is the angle $\theta,$ between the observer's line of sight to the boat and the bank, decreasing when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}6?$ Assume the angle of elevation is decreasing at a **positive** rate, and do not round the answer.

![](images/ab/abf063d149ae14c11b9ca62208a4390b32ae191418c2e0fe77f6038479fd5625.png)" :question/worked-solution "![](images/11/113109cb44fd2d10cd3b88324ed58d2ff6455a25c81b4f62eb1862b7ced03b52.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the distance between the boat and the bank and $x$ is the horizontal distance traveled by that boat after passing Peter. The quantity $y=10$ meters does not change with time because the boat is at a constant distance from the bank.

We wish to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\theta}{\textrm{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{10}{x} \\ x & =10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=8$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}6.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & ={csc}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & ={(2)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & =4\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate at which the angle $\theta$ is decreasing is $\dfrac{1}{5}$ radians per second."} {:db/id 17592186064129 :question/id #uuid "4ebd0289-b278-5352-b7bd-10ae218c43fb" :question/math-academy-id "e-735" :question/problem "Find the derivative of $y = \tan{\left(\sin(x)\right)}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = \tan u, \qquad u = \sin x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \sec^2 u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064136 :question/id #uuid "82a52178-7e95-554c-aedb-34e2f0336fa5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8341" :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
