\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cot}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity ${cot}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cot}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cot}^{2}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064858 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3541e9d4-b110-5c63-a736-7fc7f4d31791" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186330422} {:answer/id #uuid "86df8515-e1e9-50e5-8ffa-c0f477c898b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186331153} {:answer/id #uuid "9dec32d8-d9c0-5660-8378-5288983a6ac9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186331364} {:answer/id #uuid "a3922fe0-a979-577b-8dba-fd55ff68e732" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186331416} {:answer/id #uuid "f1373522-1826-5a96-a8aa-2b1480b28e0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186332069}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186331153} :answer-field/id #uuid "dc984231-74ce-5ee3-a0d9-26f2e71c9fc8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332589}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c589cab7-d081-524b-ae47-ab787d74dcb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-49273" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that ${cot}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{csc}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064859 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16897289-4603-55b3-85a9-7a4e51b12fc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186330138} {:answer/id #uuid "351bd75d-098f-5b2a-b526-a98d2a025590" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186330419} {:answer/id #uuid "50b59dc3-9cc4-5d56-8dae-d5fde6823b0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}{tan}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186330681} {:answer/id #uuid "9532f3f6-9b3e-5893-931d-79b72c8db1fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}{csc}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186331272} {:answer/id #uuid "bc8968e8-f099-5f73-8828-0a36b59f6c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186331612}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186331612} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b7347c5-9c24-53ba-ae9d-867009e5aca2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332398}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5f71f24a-4751-5945-a98f-4a541dbf6232" :question/math-academy-id "q-49275" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\int {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$ and $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{8}\int {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int {\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\right)}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int {\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\right)}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064932 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18e9e8cc-7e2c-5b9c-8895-6a0d01a94483" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{3}^{x}}{ln⁡3}+C" :db/id 17592186333213} {:answer/id #uuid "2550874f-8ee9-5a21-ad79-124324b76991" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "ln⁡({3}^{x})+C" :db/id 17592186333335} {:answer/id #uuid "602373f3-a4ef-5989-b10a-66c28e72546b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{3}^{x}ln⁡3+C" :db/id 17592186333867} {:answer/id #uuid "93360ddb-2f30-5402-b6bd-6562c3c2c6d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{3}^{x}+C" :db/id 17592186334300} {:answer/id #uuid "94f01e4b-399e-55ad-bf45-f119b26a99ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{ln⁡x}{ln⁡3}+C" :db/id 17592186334315}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333213} :answer-field/id #uuid "fb7cb00b-1c03-5bd1-8af9-27f6fe69ec11" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335676}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "709a586a-cd76-5969-9f50-4116711ad7ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-66139" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int {3}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186064941 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33cf2d14-d04d-51e3-b76e-64b8e1a665b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\text{arcsec}(8x)+C" :db/id 17592186333465} {:answer/id #uuid "3dc9dd34-b284-58b6-84db-345e4e630da9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{arcsec}(64x)+C" :db/id 17592186333571} {:answer/id #uuid "8f11fd04-9fa8-5d58-b9c9-6ab52adba008" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{arcsec}(8x)+C" :db/id 17592186334264} {:answer/id #uuid "d2244dec-f6d2-5e94-8b71-32f7eabc6720" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(8x)}{8}+C" :db/id 17592186334825} {:answer/id #uuid "d66dc866-442a-59b0-ad6e-365d928672f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(4x)}{4}+C" :db/id 17592186334866}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186334264} :answer-field/id #uuid "ae92fcf7-e93b-597c-a9c2-a8feb16ae56b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335558}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1c758c6a-6697-5dfb-b64a-bc653c6c226b" :question/math-academy-id "q-69476" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{8\,\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{8\,\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}=8\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $8x.$

So, let's substitute $u=8x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}8\int \frac{1}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =8\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(8x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064948 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18c16993-bae3-52c0-92ad-275cbeb50cdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186336262} {:answer/id #uuid "2e93c5d7-0745-5a8c-a9b3-de22c4366a79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186336481} {:answer/id #uuid "61070e19-b4f6-5780-b52f-32136383a579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9{cos}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186336909} {:answer/id #uuid "97d86c60-9434-5c84-85a6-a6f88a1b92d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186337417} {:answer/id #uuid "a8a113ac-1f7d-54a3-aa47-90b10288ae2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186337557}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336481} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a78cc6f-1a98-5e11-9c07-21ff7e2374f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338355}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "270b54b6-fdc6-5a75-af7c-f8052eee38ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-72154" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ when $f(x)=9{sin}^{2}⁡(x).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express

$$
f(x)=9(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f=9{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=18u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =18u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =18\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064952 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17153736-08a5-511b-8d66-3076de3a56f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,\text{arcsec}(2x)+C" :db/id 17592186339331} {:answer/id #uuid "287af432-ac1d-5bb0-9cce-df095ab56481" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(2x)}{4}+C" :db/id 17592186339481} {:answer/id #uuid "3031610e-8402-5eae-b837-b04a952ccb28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,\text{arcsec}(2x)+C" :db/id 17592186339548} {:answer/id #uuid "741561ed-033d-5aff-8ad7-766c99be57a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\,\text{arcsec}(2x)+C" :db/id 17592186340158} {:answer/id #uuid "c8a5cb98-9b11-5ca7-8b96-437d604616ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(2x)}{2}+C" :db/id 17592186340906}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339548} :answer-field/id #uuid "79900759-4114-5519-b212-5c813256836c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341594}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a6fafd98-c438-5a64-a87a-7a2d0a58fd7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-73717" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{2\,\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}=4\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|2x|\sqrt{(2x)^{2}-1}}.

$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186064969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00e4c1ce-4f9c-5bb7-ae3e-725c36b43eec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\pi \operatorname{coth}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186357765} {:answer/id #uuid "22b09c51-8766-5f26-aca8-a80acc80fcdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\pi \operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186358052} {:answer/id #uuid "77b6c9c7-ec92-5929-a251-3378f21e9213" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi \operatorname{csch}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186358786} {:answer/id #uuid "c25e8c9e-befc-58e3-a8e4-e8ebd1c3143f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi \operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186359457} {:answer/id #uuid "dcddbbf9-ec28-5f89-9894-25fc0c9b26c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi \operatorname{coth}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186359693}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359457} :answer-field/id #uuid "da331e09-5812-5d03-806f-1da0fe3178e9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360378}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "500d6eed-a80c-58be-9749-913f1b16bec9" :question/math-academy-id "q-95257" :question/problem "$$

\int 4{csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)=-{csch}^{2}⁡x\,⇒\,\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C.

Therefore, we have

$$"} {:db/id 17592186065360 :tutorial/content "Any number raised to the power of zero is equal to $1.$ For example,

To understand why, let's try to convince ourselves that $2^0 = 1.$ First, we write down a table containing all of the powers of $2$:

$$

$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is divided by $2$ each time. Following this pattern, we must have 

$$

It doesn't matter whether the number is positive or negative, a fraction or a decimal, big or small. To understand why dividing zero by any number (other than zero) always equals zero, think about it this way: if you have zero pizzas, and you want to divide zero pizzas among ten friends, then each friend will get exactly zero pizza." :tutorial/id #uuid "65c0e3ec-7962-5911-a3c9-9de126e87edc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3120 :tutorial/title "Dividing Zero by Another Number"} {:db/id 17592186065364 :tutorial/content "Division by zero is **undefined.** No number can be divided by zero, not even zero itself.

To see why, notice that if we divide $6$ by $3$, we get

Therefore, ? is not a number." :tutorial/id #uuid "d8152649-f215-53b2-9811-ce74f0d61dc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3121 :tutorial/title "Dividing by Zero is Undefined"} {:db/id 17592186065381 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we learned how to use substitution to evaluate integrals that give rise to inverse trigonometric functions.

Although you can always solve these integrals by going through the substitution process, it is convenient to remember the following key results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(ax)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(ax)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{{a}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{|ax|\sqrt{(ax)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\text{arcsec}(ax)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To remember the results above, note the following:

- Whenever the integrand has an $ax$ term, the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $ax.$

- Otherwise, if the $a$ and $x$ are separated, then the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $\dfrac{x}{a}.$

- All the results are multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{a},$ except for $\arcsin \left( \dfrac{x}{a} \right) + C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02539765-4345-5409-87f9-9901a59b7ebf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4800 :tutorial/title "Summary of Key Results"} {:db/id 17592186065390 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

We know that the derivative of the hyperbolic sine is the hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sinh{x}) = \cosh{x}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we have

$$
\int \cosh{x}\,\textrm d x = \sinh{x} + C.
$$

Similarly, by considering the derivative of the hyperbolic cosine, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\cosh x) = \sinh{x} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \int \sinh x\  \textrm{d}x = \cosh x + C.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d780519f-20fa-5840-be56-4a5f0539ed6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5211 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065392 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

By considering the derivatives of the hyperbolic tangent, secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C \\ \int \operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡x+C \\ \int {csch}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e3a8b50-3176-54c9-a9a3-e21f958ab6b2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5371 :tutorial/title "Integration Using Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions"} {:db/id 17592186065409 :tutorial/content "We know that the derivative of sine is cosine:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sin{x}) = \cos{x}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we see that the integral of cosine is sine:

$$
\int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C
$$

We can discover two other integrals by considering the derivatives of cosine and tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, by considering the derivatives of secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

With these six formulas, we can integrate many different trigonometric functions." :tutorial/id #uuid "bfa0c70d-6cf7-5c69-8995-d9f6c980a4ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 718 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065410 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsin}x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arctan}x) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{arcsec}\,x) & =\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the opposite of differentiation, we arrive at the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcsin}(x)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arctan}(x)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =\text{arcsec}(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a238ada9-9756-56cd-992d-a26ce54ab913" :tutorial/math-academy-id 723 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065416 :tutorial/content "Dividing with negative numbers follows similar rules as multiplying with negative numbers. 

First of all, a negative number divided by a positive number gives a negative number. We can picture this rule as

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,÷\,(+)\,=\,(-).\end{aligned}
$$

For example, let's use this rule to find the value of $(-6) \div 2.$

Here, since we are dividing a negative number $\color{red}(-6)$ by a positive number ${\color{blue}(2)},$ the result is going to be negative:
$$
{\color{red}(-6)} \div {\color{blue}2} = {\color{red} \mathbf{-} \boxed{ {\phantom{3}}} }
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $6$ by $2$ *without* any signs: $6 \div 2 = 3.$ So, we get

$$
{\color{red}(-6)} \div {\color{blue}2} = {\color{red} -3 }.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b92ac2e4-b983-5fd5-bc18-7dfb821497f0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8108 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065417 :tutorial/content "A positive number divided by a negative number is also a negative number. We can picture this rule as

$$
\begin{aligned}(+)\,÷\,(-)\,=\,(-).\end{aligned}
$$

For instance, to find $8\div (-2),$ we have to divide a positive number $\color{blue}(8)$ by a negative one ${\color{red}(-2)}.$ So the result will be negative:
$$
{\color{blue}8} \div {\color{red}(-2)} = {\color{red}\mathbf{-} \boxed{ {\phantom{10}}} }
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $8$ by $2$ without any signs: $8 \div 2 = 4.$ So, we get

$$
{\color{blue}8} \div {\color{red}(-2)} = {\color{red}-4}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "67beb927-7da4-5576-8982-1a823c878691" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8109 :tutorial/title "The Quotient of a Positive and a Negative is a Negative"} {:db/id 17592186065418 :tutorial/content "Finally, the third rule is that a negative number divided by a negative number is a positive number:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,÷\,(-)\,=\,(+)\end{aligned}
$$

To demonstrate, let's find $-12 \div (-3).$ We have to divide a negative number $\color{red}(-12)$ by another negative number ${\color{red}(-3)}.$ So the result will be positive:
$$
{\color{red}(-12)} \div {\color{red}(-3)} = {\color{blue} \boxed{ {\phantom{4}}} }
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $12$ by $3$ without any signs: $12 \div 3 = 4.$ Therefore,  we get

$$
{\color{red}(-12)} \div {\color{red}(-3)} = {\color{blue}4}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b1d3d95e-7953-5c5b-b97b-d4eb85e1f80d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8111 :tutorial/title "The Quotient of a Negative and a Negative is a Positive"} {:db/id 17592186065421 :tutorial/content "Let's think about how to simplify the following:

$$
\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}
$$

 

The expression above is a fraction, but there are additional fractions in the numerator and denominator.
Such expressions are called **fractions of fractions**.
We use parentheses to make it easier to read.

The trick to working with fractions of fractions is to remember that a fraction represents a division. So, a fraction of fractions is a division of two fractions:

$$
\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}\right)} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \boldsymbol{\div} \left(\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}\right)
$$

Now, recall that dividing by $\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}$ is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal $\dfrac{\color{red}{4}}{\color{blue}{3}}.$ We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)÷\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) &= \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\times \left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \\ &= \frac{2\times 4}{3\times 3} \\ &= \frac{8}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{8}{9}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5da17ec4-93cc-5398-bbfc-d50405cd2fad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8182 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065435 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to calculate the integral

$$
\displaystyle \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

At first glance, this looks kind of tricky. However, if we use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x,$ we can rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x &=\int {\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\right)}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we see that this is just a standard trigonometric integral:

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x  =  \int\csc^2 x\,\textrm d x =-\cot x + C
$$

When confronted with a tricky-looking trigonometric integral, we can often reduce it to a standard integral using a trigonometric identity." :tutorial/id #uuid "d2dcb6a2-e8f7-5bb7-9450-e0b65532681a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 867 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "9c8edcdc-8f1c-51c2-bbb5-0e9493ab87c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}arcsec(x + 3) + C" :db/id 17592186066869} {:answer/id #uuid "b6844ac0-a966-53fc-be83-d306677a8eb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "arcsec(x - \displaystyle{\int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    x^2-2x&= x^2 -2x +(1-1)\\[3pt]
              &= (x^2 -2x +1)-1\\[3pt]
         &= (x-1)^2-1
         
  \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x 
= \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{(x-1)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec} \, u +C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x-1$.

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x-1.
$$

 
Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u$.

&=  \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3}\dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{(x-1)^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt]
&=\int_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2} \dfrac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
&=  \textrm{arcsec}\, {u}\Big|_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2}\\[5pt]
&= \textrm{arcsec} \left(2\right)  - \textrm{arcsec}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right)\\[5pt]
&=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.

\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186068569 :question/id #uuid "234c7a86-037c-5316-9419-14db90d1da60" :question/math-academy-id "e-466" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int x^2 \sec^2\left(x^3-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\,\textrm d x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186068570 :question/id #uuid "03e461a3-0fe0-5fb5-813e-ae23a5dc606a" :question/math-academy-id "e-467" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186068580 :question/id #uuid "5b83575b-9674-5dc5-b3eb-a918f145be93" :question/math-academy-id "e-497" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \dfrac{\ln^2{x}}{x} \textrm{d}x
$$ using integration by parts." :question/worked-solution "First, we let

$$
I = \int \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\right)\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{3}⁡x-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{3}⁡x-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{3}⁡x-2I \\ 3I & ={ln}^{3}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186068597 :question/id #uuid "4fba84c9-6c0f-51cd-b5f2-8b469bd8346f" :question/math-academy-id "e-5135" :question/problem "What is the result of dividing $\dfrac 3 x$ by $\dfrac y {6x^2}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$

Note that in the final step, we canceled out a common factor of $x$ in the numerator and denominator."} {:db/id 17592186068598 :question/id #uuid "fa6bbedb-654a-58a5-8fcf-3bb0fd038160" :question/math-academy-id "e-5136" :question/problem "Given that $\dfrac {2a^2(1+b)} {3b}  =x$ and $\dfrac {1+b}{5b^2} =y ,$ then what is $x \div y?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute $x \div y,$ i.e.,

$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac {2a^2(1+b)} {3b}  \div  \dfrac{1+b}{5b^2} &= \dfrac {2a^2(1+b)} {3b}  \cdot  \dfrac {5b^2} {1+b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {2a^2\cancel{(1+b)}} {3\cancel{b}}  \cdot  \dfrac {5b^{\cancel{2}}} {\cancel{1+b}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {10a^2b} {3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186068604 :question/id #uuid "dd8b5378-4da1-5955-a566-f84ef0cecb28" :question/math-academy-id "e-5206" :question/problem "What is the result of dividing $\dfrac 3 x$ by $\dfrac {5}{y}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186068605 :question/id #uuid "3fd58494-e5ee-5dc7-af3c-959888f59627" :question/math-academy-id "e-5207" :question/problem "Given that $\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  =x$ and $\dfrac {2a} {14b^2}=y,$ then what is $x \div y?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

$$
\begin{aligned}

		\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  &\div  \dfrac {2a} {14b^2},
	\end{aligned}
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  \div  \dfrac {2a} {14b^2} &= \dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  \cdot \dfrac {14b^2} {2a} \\ &= \dfrac {2a(a^2 - 5)} {7b}  \cdot  \dfrac {2b \cdot 7b} {2a} \\ &= \dfrac {\cancel{2a}(a^2 - 5)} {\cancel{7b}}  \cdot  \dfrac {2b \cdot \cancel{7b}} {\cancel{2a}} \\ &= \dfrac {2b(a^2 - 5)} 1 \\ &= 2a^2b - 10b\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186068622 :question/id #uuid "68d38626-1153-51ec-a3c6-d39c927fdd99" :question/math-academy-id "e-600" :question/problem "A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x =  \sin(2t), \qquad y= 2\cos (2t) \qquad 0 \leq t \lt \pi.
$$

Given that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = -2 \tan(2t),$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}$ at the point where $t=\dfrac\pi 8.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y }{\textrm d x^2},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)}.\end{aligned}

We're given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= -2 \tan(2t),$ and we can calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} ( \sin 2t ) = 2 \cos(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-2\operatorname{tan}⁡2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8},$ and we get

$$"} {:db/id 17592186069046 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a9ba381-dfc6-54d8-b261-945875616b86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3})+C" :db/id 17592186266662} {:answer/id #uuid "9828aecd-8ee6-528b-84cd-c4bcd17317b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡({x}^{3})+C" :db/id 17592186267508} {:answer/id #uuid "c2c830ad-dfcc-5ddf-a4bf-a03b19a9f887" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3})+C" :db/id 17592186267881} {:answer/id #uuid "f14834f1-3a8c-5e06-be70-0657e9f80ea7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3})+C" :db/id 17592186268290} {:answer/id #uuid "fe106718-50d2-53cd-a30d-c21520e167e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3})+C" :db/id 17592186268381}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186268381} :answer-field/id #uuid "19c18458-8765-5ccd-8e3b-95cdb8f39a5e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268448}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a1978088-009a-552d-a613-5fc9a66c590e" :question/math-academy-id "q-13474" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u={x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we have

17592186377321}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6c2769dd-8773-5498-9a3b-b2fed58e581f" :question/math-academy-id "q-3400" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡(x))\left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\text{d}x.
$$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))\left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+(-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C) \\  & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}(2{ln}^{2}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186069401 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8493e63b-e686-55a1-be24-8c7387ac529a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e" :db/id 17592186067577} {:answer/id #uuid "b510294a-158b-59cf-9325-faaa6db5c999" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186067579} {:answer/id #uuid "b70392a5-b997-5c61-a383-809b3402a781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186067580} {:answer/id #uuid "547cd2d2-426a-5ed4-ba68-b0d437d86899" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186067581} {:answer/id #uuid "1c227681-1e75-580c-a1f0-afa6524eba89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e-1" :db/id 17592186547373}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186067579} :answer-field/id #uuid "2656a382-672f-58cb-ac31-49e3432a71cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186067576}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d20f7fe1-3115-57de-8eab-3a56c473cbe5" :question/math-academy-id "q-49976" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z
$$ using integration by parts." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $$
\displaystyle I=\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{3}⁡z\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=\frac{3{ln}^{2}⁡z}{z}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}=\frac{1}{z}\, & ⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z=\operatorname{ln}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={ln}^{3}⁡z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z)\left(\frac{3{ln}^{2}⁡z}{z}\right)\,\text{d}z \\  & ={ln}^{4}⁡z-3\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{4}⁡z-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{4}⁡z-3I \\ 4I & ={ln}^{4}⁡z \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡z}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{1}{4}({ln}^{4}⁡z){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({ln}^{4}⁡(e)-{ln}^{4}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186069412 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ded48646-180c-5b0b-a6e9-fca073f5a695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186067645} {:answer/id #uuid "0f6a5f44-7c10-57f2-8e95-6bb68e1b82b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186427576} {:answer/id #uuid "2331cd21-2ed1-5625-a66c-71e5cb90700e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{2},\,2⟩" :db/id 17592186427578} {:answer/id #uuid "4ac18ed6-58a3-5417-b730-cedc5302f322" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,\,2⟩" :db/id 17592186427580} {:answer/id #uuid "a96be7b9-8d6b-519e-93fb-b0e6acf1e4a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186427584}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427584} :answer-field/id #uuid "2aea7a53-b7bf-5584-8696-8766da29f419" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186067642}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2dc454b1-c8a7-57a0-a955-d54808121033" :question/math-academy-id "q-50359" :question/problem "Given that $r(t)=⟨{cos}^{2}⁡t,\,{sin}^{2}⁡t⟩,$ calculate $r\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right).$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into our function, and we get

Just like with fractions!

For example, let's divide $x$ by $\dfrac{3}{y}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x \div \dfrac{3}{y}
$$

To do this, we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. The divisor is $\dfrac{3}{y},$ and to get the reciprocal, we just flip the fraction upside down: $\dfrac{y}{3}.$ Multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x÷\frac{3}{y} &= x\cdot \frac{y}{3} \\ &= \frac{xy}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see some more examples!" :tutorial/id #uuid "67b283bf-2859-595a-bacb-ebf32b5f7275" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3379 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186070032 :tutorial/content "In some cases, applying integration by parts can lead to a cyclic pattern, where the original integral reappears after a few steps. This cyclic behavior allows us to solve the integral by forming an equation that can be solved algebraically.

To illustrate, let's consider the following example:

$$
I = \int \dfrac{\ln x}{x} \textrm{d}x
$$

Let's try using the method of integration by parts. We suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x-\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x-I\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the same integral $I$ on both sides of the equality. Thinking about $I$ as some unknown variable, we can easily solve this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{2}⁡x-I \\ I+I & ={ln}^{2}⁡x \\ 2I & ={ln}^{2}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{2}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we added a constant of integration right at the very end of the calculation." :tutorial/id #uuid "eac7b2d2-bdab-56e5-bb03-00e69bb0caf6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 904 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "e0b6d410-7e03-5a85-9087-1b510c6f5829" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3 \div \frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186070221} {:answer/id #uuid "49fded30-4d53-505e-a0f8-70202f8261d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4} \div 3" :db/id 17592186070222} {:answer/id #uuid "95b9c4f0-c504-563e-a3ca-331f61c8d461" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3} \div 7" :db/id 17592186070225} {:answer/id #uuid "752d6ba5-2e0b-5e3a-904c-2e7bb8319db3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7 \div \frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186070228} {:answer/id #uuid "e312c331-19bc-5692-a649-3c55982b9227" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3} \div 5 = \frac{5}{15}" :db/id 17592186072405} {:answer/id #uuid "e9ebc581-a21e-5517-b2f5-be49a147ce4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3} \div 5 = \frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186072406} {:answer/id #uuid "17f20138-3358-5ecd-a9e1-c314f1e1cbba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5} \div 3 = \frac{1}{15}" :db/id 17592186072407} {:answer/id #uuid "45ab3164-0f59-5b22-8750-5602e97cd92c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5} \div 3 = \frac{3}{15}" :db/id 17592186072408} {:answer/id #uuid "75342c65-c405-5c24-9571-a7e728645e8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5} \div 3 = \frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186072409} {:db/id 17592186073415 :question/id #uuid "3deda9a1-7edd-5b1e-9f39-5c69644f30ab" :question/math-academy-id "e-10542" :question/problem "Greg stacked $5$ cardboard boxes on top of each other. If the ham is distributed equally among the $4$ pizzas, how much ham does he put on each pizza?" :question/worked-solution "To determine the amount of ham on each pizza, we must divide the amount of ham by the number of pizzas:

\dfrac{1}{2} \div 4
$$

Therefore, Joshua puts $\dfrac{1}{8} \, \textrm{kg}$ of ham on each pizza."} {:db/id 17592186073467 :question/id #uuid "dd5b4bc8-110c-5247-b5e6-ee4ce7636a1b" :question/math-academy-id "e-13707" :question/problem "Each of the three shapes in the model below represents one whole.

\boxed{ {\hspace{0.167em} \phantom{0} \hspace{0.167em}}} \div \dfrac{1}{4} = \boxed{ {\hspace{0.167em} \phantom{0} \hspace{0.167em}}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "In the model, there are $\color{red}3$ shapes. Each shape consists of $4$ pieces that each represent $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of a whole. There are $\color{blue}12$ pieces in total.

The model above represents $3$ wholes. Use this model to calculate the value of $3 \div \dfrac{1}{5}.$" :question/worked-solution "To calculate ${\color{red}3} \div \dfrac{1}{\color{blue}5}$, we need to divide each of $\color{red}3$ wholes into $\color{blue}5$ equal parts, as shown below.

![](images/32/327833c4954c43c2093cb31a03cef01e66389e7cafc3bb2d4cd174e0f7e64f5d.png)

Therefore:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186073469 :question/id #uuid "469cedf6-ef5d-5dcd-902e-418b6f19e347" :question/math-academy-id "e-13723" :question/problem "Divide $14 \div \dfrac{1}{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "To divide a whole number by a unit fraction, we multiply the whole number by the fraction's denominator:

If each pizza needs $\dfrac{1}{10}$ of a kilogram of wheat flour, how many pizzas can Johnny make?" :question/worked-solution "To determine the number of pizzas that Johnny can make, we divide the amount of wheat flour by the amount of wheat flour each pizza needs.

Therefore, $206.6 \div 3.43$ is approximately equal to $69$."} {:db/id 17592186073479 :question/id #uuid "b223571e-3070-5474-a01c-f909c89bf36d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13900" :question/problem "Estimate the value of $116.8 \div 5.15$ by rounding each number to the nearest whole number. Round your final answer to the nearest whole number." :question/worked-solution "We round both numbers to the nearest whole number:
$$
\begin{array}{ccc}116.8 & ÷ & 5.15 \\ ↓ &  & ↓ \\ {\color{blue}{117}} & ÷ & {\color{blue}{5}}\end{array}
$$

Now, we need to find the value of
$117\div 5$.

So, we go through the long division procedure as usual:

|  |  | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $5$ | $\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 1 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 7}$ |  |  |
| $-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$ | $1$ | $0$ |  |
|  |  | $1$ | $7$ |
|  | $-\!\!\!\!\!$ | $1$ | $5$ |
|  |  |  | $\fbox{2}$ |

Therefore,

$$
117 \div 5 = 23\,\text{R}2
$$

The remainder $2$ is closer to $0$ than to the divisor $5$. So, to round to the nearest whole number, we must round down:

$$
117 \div 5 \rightarrow 23
$$

Therefore, $116.8 \div 5.15$ is approximately equal to $23$."} {:db/id 17592186073486 :question/id #uuid "4fae5cf1-65c9-5217-89ec-54b40e80f293" :question/math-academy-id "e-14418" :question/problem "What division problem is represented by the model below?

![](images/b2/b2e5fb40e703cb3d93f22fd315852930eaab540445e3f570e8de3dacfdc83e0b.png)" :question/worked-solution "We have $\dfrac{1}{4}$ on the left and $\dfrac{1}{8}$ on the right.

The division operation splits the shaded region on the left into $2$ equal parts. So the shaded part on the left is $2$ times larger than the shaded part on the right.

$$"} {:db/id 17592186073487 :question/id #uuid "9cd2d717-01de-5319-8759-2990e79d64ad" :question/math-academy-id "e-14420" :question/problem "What number is missing from the division problem below?

![](images/cf/cf2500f82f337e5635a5ca9854579e3b883f42cde4598d4324c94364bf998a0d.png)" :question/worked-solution "We have $\dfrac{1}{3}$ on the left and $\dfrac{1}{15}$ on the right.

So, the missing number is $\color{blue}5.$"} {:db/id 17592186073489 :question/id #uuid "c6e1860a-9fe5-559c-8a19-6ed98335659b" :question/math-academy-id "e-14424" :question/problem "Use the model below to calculate $\dfrac{1}{4} \div 4.$

![](images/8e/8eccf163bffabb43593188590a1f995544f3d1ac0aebcdd87dce638b230f8165.png)" :question/worked-solution "Since we need to divide by $\color{blue}4$, we split the whole into $\color{blue}4$ equal parts horizontally.

![](images/a3/a34a3fb198ef2ea79f8baf8f0acbdbdc179c6259c614824315d3d96e5ea4e921.png)

From the picture on the right, we obtain that the shaded part represents $\dfrac{1}{16}$ of the whole.

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{1}{4} \div 4 = \dfrac{1}{16}\,.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186073503 :question/id #uuid "6247fce4-259e-5569-bbdf-b88cc1ea9482" :question/math-academy-id "e-14515" :question/problem "Tom and Margaret went to a fruit store to buy apples and pears. Tom bought $3$ kilograms of apples while Margaret bought $\dfrac{11}{3}$ kilograms of pears. Expressing the result as a mixed number, how many kilograms of fruit did they buy together?" :question/worked-solution "To know how many kilograms they bought, we have to calculate the sum:

$$
3 + \dfrac{11}{3}
$$

To add

$$
3 + \dfrac{11}{\color{blue}{3}}
$$

, we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of ${\color{blue}{3}}$.

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\dfrac{3}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $\color{blue}3$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by ${\color{blue}{3}}$:

$$
\dfrac{3 \times {\color{blue}{3}}}{1 \times{\color{blue}{3}}} = \dfrac{9}{3}
$$

So now, we have to find the following sum:

$$
\dfrac{9}{3} + \dfrac{11}{3}
$$

To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same.

$$
\frac{9}{3} + \frac{11}{3} = \frac{9 + 11}{3} = \frac{20}{3}
$$

Finally, we convert this to a mixed number:

$$
20 \div 3 = 6 \, \textrm{R} \, 2 = 6 \, \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

Thus, Tom and Margaret bought

$$
6 \, \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

kilograms of fruit."} {:db/id 17592186073522 :question/id #uuid "d566c6a3-426d-591e-a884-16ff5e10a825" :question/math-academy-id "e-1745" :question/problem "What is $\dfrac{31}{9} - 2$ expressed as a mixed number?" :question/worked-solution "To subtract $2$ from

$$
\dfrac{31}{\color{blue}{9}}
$$

, we need to express the whole number $2$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of ${\color{blue}{9}}$.

First, we write $2$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\dfrac{2}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $\color{blue}9$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by ${\color{blue}{9}}$:

$$
\dfrac{2 \times {\color{blue}{9}}}{1\times{\color{blue}{9}}} = \dfrac{18}{9}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\dfrac{31}{9} - \dfrac{18}{9}
$$

To subtract two fractions with like denominators, we subtract the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{31}{9} - \frac{18}{9} = \frac{31 - 18}{9} = \frac{13}{9}
$$

Finally, we convert to a mixed number:

$$
13 \div 9 = 1 \, \textrm{R} \, 4
$$

So our final answer is

$$
1 \, \dfrac{4}{9}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186073523 :question/id #uuid "f6f05542-54f4-5fc6-807b-b012abcfaa70" :question/math-academy-id "e-1747" :question/problem "Julia had $4$ liters of orange juice, but she accidentally spilled $\dfrac{15}{8}$ liters of juice. Expressed as a mixed number, how much juice is left?" :question/worked-solution "To find out how much juice is left, we have to calculate the difference

$$
4 - \dfrac{15}{8}
$$

To subtract

$$
\dfrac{15}{\color{blue}{8}}
$$

from $4$, we need to express the whole number $4$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of ${\color{blue}{8}}$.

First, we write $4$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\dfrac{4}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $\color{blue}8$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by ${\color{blue}{8}}$:

$$
\dfrac{4 \times {\color{blue}{8}}}{1\times{\color{blue}{8}}} = \dfrac{32}{8}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\dfrac{32}{8} - \dfrac{15}{8}
$$

To subtract two fractions with like denominators, we subtract the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{32}{8} - \frac{15}{8} = \frac{32 - 15}{8} = \frac{17}{8}
$$

Finally, we convert to a mixed number:

$$
17 \div 8 = 2 \, \textrm{R} \, 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
2 \, \dfrac{1}{8}
$$

liters of juice is left."} {:db/id 17592186073524 :question/id #uuid "83452ea8-bf0c-54eb-8ed5-54bb3c200d2d" :question/math-academy-id "e-1812" :question/problem "Harold cuts an $85$-inch long rope into $5$ pieces of the same size. How long is each piece?" :question/worked-solution "To find out how long each of the pieces is, we need to divide $85$ by $5$.

We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $5$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$ |  |
| --- | ---: |

First, we consider the tens:

| $\color{blue}1$$5$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}8} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$5$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$3$$\color{lightgray}5$ | Divide: ${\color{red}8} \div 5 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,3$Write over tens: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $5 \times {\color{blue}1} = 5$Subtract: ${\color{red}8} - 5 = 3$Bring down: $5$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the ones:

| $1$$\color{blue}7$$5$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$5$$\color{red}3$$\color{red}5$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$3$$5$$\fbox{0}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}35} \div 5 = {\color{blue}7}$Write over ones: $\color{blue}7$Multiply: $5 \times {\color{blue}7} = 35$Subtract: ${\color{red}35} - 35 = \fbox{0}$ |
| --- | ---: |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $85$, so the division is done.

Therefore,

$$
85 \div 5 = 17
$$

This means that each piece of rope is $17$ inches long."} {:db/id 17592186073525 :question/id #uuid "00006ac6-b956-55b9-9bac-e83cdee6e998" :question/math-academy-id "e-1813" :question/problem "From top to bottom, what are the missing digits in the following division problem?

| $\fbox{\phantom{1}}$$2$$7$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!$$\fbox{\phantom{7}}$$\fbox{\phantom{1}}$$5$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$1$$4$$1$ |
| --- |" :question/worked-solution "We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $7$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$ |  |
| --- | ---: |

First, we consider the tens:

| $\color{blue}1$$7$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}8} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$7$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$1$$\color{lightgray}5$ | Divide: ${\color{red}8} \div 7 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,1$Write over tens: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $7 \times {\color{blue}1} = 7$Subtract: ${\color{red}8} - 7 = 1$Bring down: $5$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the ones:

| $1$$\color{blue}2$$7$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$7$$\color{red}1$$\color{red}5$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$1$$4$$\fbox{1}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}15} \div 7 = {\color{blue}2}\,\text{R}\,1$Write over ones: $\color{blue}2$Multiply: $7 \times {\color{blue}2} = 14$Subtract: ${\color{red}15} - 14 = \fbox{1}$ |
| --- | ---: |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $85$, so the division is done. However, we still have a remainder of $1$, so we include this in our final answer.

Therefore,

$$

$$

The missing digits are $1$, $7$ and $1$:

| $\fbox{1}$$2$$7$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!$$\fbox{7}$$\fbox{1}$$5$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$1$$4$$1$ |
| --- |"} {:db/id 17592186073526 :question/id #uuid "c4ce9599-6ea0-5f35-ba9a-eb7f1ad42ab4" :question/math-academy-id "e-1814" :question/problem "What is $86$ divided by $2$?" :question/worked-solution "We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $\color{blue}4$$2$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}8} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 6}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$0$$\color{lightgray}6$ | Divide: ${\color{red}8} \div 2 = {\color{blue}4}$Write over tens: $\color{blue}4$Multiply: $2 \times {\color{blue}4} = 8$Subtract: ${\color{red}8} - 8 = 0$Bring down: $6$ |

Next, we consider the ones:

| $4$$\color{blue}3$$2$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 6}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$0$$\color{red}6$$-\!\!\!\!$$6$$\fbox{0}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}6} \div 2 = {\color{blue}3}$Write over ones: $\color{blue}3$Multiply: $2 \times {\color{blue}3} = 6$Subtract: ${\color{red}6} - 6 = \fbox{0}$ |
| --- | ---: |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $86$, so the division is done.

Therefore,

$$
86 \div 2 = 43
$$"} {:db/id 17592186073527 :question/id #uuid "231a328c-fcbb-56c0-b0f7-40dc68bc34bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-1815" :question/problem "Find the quotient and the remainder of $89\div 6$." :question/worked-solution "We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 9}$ |  |
| --- | ---: |

First, we consider the tens:

| $\color{blue}1$$6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}8} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 9}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$6$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$2$$\color{lightgray}9$ | Divide: ${\color{red}8} \div 6 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,2$Write over tens: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $6 \times {\color{blue}1} = 6$Subtract: ${\color{red}8} - 6 = 2$Bring down: $9$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the ones:

| $1$$\color{blue}4$$6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 9}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$6$$\color{red}2$$\color{red}9$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$2$$4$$\fbox{5}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}29} \div 6 = {\color{blue}4}\,\text{R}\,5$Write over ones: $\color{blue}4$Multiply: $6 \times {\color{blue}4} = 24$Subtract: ${\color{red}29} - 24 = \fbox{5}$ |
| --- | ---: |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $89$, so the division is done. However, we still have a remainder of $5$, so we include this in our final answer.

Therefore,

$$
89 \div 6 = 14\,\text{R}\,5
$$"} {:db/id 17592186073528 :question/id #uuid "b83956c9-d606-5ce0-bc37-c00a9498e61f" :question/math-academy-id "e-1819" :question/problem "What is $847 \div 6$?" :question/worked-solution "We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 4 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 7}$ |  |

First, we consider the hundreds:

| $\color{blue}1$$6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}8} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 4 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 7}$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$6$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$2$$\color{lightgray}4$ | Divide: ${\color{red}8} \div 6 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,2$Write over hundreds: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $6 \times {\color{blue}1} = 6$Subtract: ${\color{red}8} - 6 = 2$Bring down: $4$ |

Next, we consider the tens:

| $1$$\color{blue}4$$6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 4 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 7}$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$6$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$\color{red}2$$\color{red}4$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$2$$4$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$0$$\color{lightgray}7$ | Divide: ${\color{red}24} \div 6 = {\color{blue}4}$Write over tens: $\color{blue}4$Multiply: $6 \times {\color{blue}4} = 24$Subtract: ${\color{red}24} - 24 = 0$Bring down: $7$ |
| --- | ---: |

Finally, we consider the ones:

| $1$$4$$\color{blue}1$$6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{8 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 4 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 7}$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$6$$2$$4$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$2$$4$$0$$\color{red}7$$-\!\!\!$$6$$\fbox{1}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}7} \div 6 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,1$Write over ones: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $6 \times {\color{blue}1} = 6$Subtract: ${\color{red}7} - 6 = \fbox{1}$ |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $847$, so the division is done. However, we still have a remainder of $1$, so we include this in our final answer.

Therefore,

$$
847 \div 6 = 141\,\text{R}\,1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186073529 :question/id #uuid "99d7e5f9-0989-54d9-aa02-4a4a97365176" :question/math-academy-id "e-1820" :question/problem "Find the **quotient** in the following long division problem:
$6 \: \enclose{longdiv}{3 \: 7\: 9}$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $\color{red}3$ (the number of hundreds in ${\color{red}3}79$) is less than the divisor $6$. Therefore, we should consider both the hundreds and tens:

| $\color{blue}6$$6$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}3} {\:\phantom{\mid}} {\color{red}7} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 9}$$-\!\!\!$$3$$6$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$1$$\color{lightgray}9$ | Divide: ${\color{red}37} \div 6 = {\color{blue}6}\,\text{R}\,1$Write over tens: $\color{blue}6$Multiply: $6 \times {\color{blue}6} = 36$Subtract: ${\color{red}37} - 36 = 1$Bring down: $9$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the ones:

$$

To find the unit rate of minutes per pool, we divide the number of minutes, $15,$ by the total pool volume emptied, $\dfrac{3}{2},$ as follows:

$$
15 \div \dfrac{3}{2}
$$

To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the fraction's reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}15÷\frac{3}{2} & =15\times \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{15}{1}\times \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{15\times 2}{1\times 3} \\  & =\frac{30}{3} \\  & =30÷3 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

So, the unit rate is $10$ minutes per pool. To find the number of minutes that the pump takes to empty $5$ pools, we multiply the unit rate by $5$ pools and get

$$

$$

To find the unit rate of dollars per liter, we divide the number of dollars, $\dfrac{3}{4},$ by the number of liters, $\dfrac{3}{8},$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac{3}{8}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}÷\frac{3}{8} & =\frac{3}{4}\times \frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\times 8}{4\times 3} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =24÷12 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the unit rate is $2$ dollars per liter. To find the number of dollars that Ava earns selling $18$ liters, we multiply the unit rate by $18$ liters and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\times 18 & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-92461" :question/problem "Estimate $6.4 \div 97.7$ by rounding the divisor to the nearest hundred."} {:db/id 17592186074942 :tutorial/content "When we compare two ratios, we are comparing how much one quantity is associated with another quantity.

One way to compare ratios is to write each ratio as a fraction and simplify.

For example, suppose Store A has $12$ pens and $3$ notebooks, and Store B has $15$ pens and $5$ notebooks.

The ratio of pens to notebooks at Store A is $12:3,$ which can be written as

$$
\dfrac{12}{3}.
$$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing the numerator and denominator by $3{:}$

$$
\dfrac{12 \div 3}{3 \div 3} = \dfrac{4}{1} = 4
$$

So the ratio $12:3$ is equivalent to $4:1.$

The ratio of pens to notebooks at Store B is $15:5,$ which can be written as

$$
\dfrac{15}{5}.
$$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing the numerator and denominator by $5{:}$

$$
\dfrac{15 \div 5}{5 \div 5} = \dfrac{3}{1} = 3
$$

So the ratio $15:5$ is equivalent to $3:1.$

Since $4 > 3,$ Store A has a larger ratio of pens to notebooks than Store B." :tutorial/id #uuid "7bc4123c-1fa8-5a6d-bc95-a6f15b553510" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14911 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074944 :tutorial/content "Sometimes it is helpful to compare two ratios by writing them as fractions.

To do this, write each ratio as a fraction, simplify, and then compare the simplified fractions.

For example, suppose Jar A has $3$ blue marbles and $24$ red marbles, and Jar B has $5$ blue marbles and $20$ red marbles.

The ratio of blue marbles to red marbles in Jar A is $3:24,$ which can be written as

$$
\dfrac{3}{24}.
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $3{:}$

$$
\dfrac{3 \div 3}{24 \div 3} = \dfrac{1}{8}
$$

The ratio of blue marbles to red marbles in Jar B is $5:20,$ which can be written as

$$
\dfrac{5}{20}.
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $5{:}$

$$
\dfrac{5 \div 5}{20 \div 5} = \dfrac{1}{4}
$$

To compare $\dfrac{1}{8}$ and $\dfrac{1}{4},$ we look at the denominators. Since $8$ is larger than $4,$ the fraction $\dfrac{1}{8}$ represents a smaller portion.

Since $\dfrac{1}{8} < \dfrac{1}{4},$ Jar A has a smaller ratio of blue marbles to red marbles than Jar B." :tutorial/id #uuid "4c852a17-40f7-57ea-a528-63625c0b469d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14913 :tutorial/title "Comparing Ratios Using Fractions"} {:db/id 17592186074950 :tutorial/content "We use the **standard algorithm** to divide a two-digit number by a one-digit number. To illustrate, let's divide $92$ by $4$.

We start by writing down the question using long division notation, as follows:

| $4$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{9 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 2}$ |  |
| --- | ---: |

First, we consider the tens. How many times does $4$ go into ${\color{red}9}$? It goes in ${\color{blue}2}$ times, and

$$
4\times {\color{blue}2} =8
$$

so there is a remainder of

$$
{\color{red}9} - 8 = 1
$$

We write the ${\color{blue}2}$ above the tens, the $8$ at the bottom, and subtract to get the remainder of $1$. Then we bring the ones digit ($2$) down next to the remainder.

| $\color{blue}2$$4$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}9} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 2}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$1$$\color{lightgray}2$ | Divide: ${\color{red}9} \div 4 = {\color{blue}2}\,\text{R}\,1$Write over tens: $\color{blue}2$Multiply: $4 \times {\color{blue}2} = 8$Subtract: ${\color{red}9} - 8 = 1$Bring down: $2$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the ones. How many times does $4$ go into ${\color{red}12}$? It goes in ${\color{blue}3}$ times, and

$$
4\times {\color{blue}3} =12
$$

so there is no remainder (

$$
{\color{red}12} - 12 = 0
$$

).

We write the ${\color{blue}3}$ above the ones, the $12$ at the bottom, and subtract to get the final remainder of $0$.

| $2$$\color{blue}3$$4$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{9 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 2}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$\color{red}1$$\color{red}2$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$1$$2$$\fbox{0}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}12} \div 4 = {\color{blue}3}$Write over ones: $\color{blue}3$Multiply: $4 \times {\color{blue}3} = 12$Subtract: ${\color{red}12} - 12 = \fbox{0}$ |
| --- | ---: |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $92$, so the division is done. The number we have written at the top is the answer.

Therefore,

$$
92 \div 4 = 23
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ee791847-fab3-56fb-889d-2d02d7dea9e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1861 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074951 :tutorial/content "If there is a remainder after using the standard algorithm, we write the remainder in the answer. To illustrate, let's find the remainder of $95\div 8\,$.

We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $8$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{9 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$ |  |
| --- | ---: |

First, we consider the tens:

| $\color{blue}1$$8$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}9} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$1$$\color{lightgray}5$ | Divide: ${\color{red}9} \div 8 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,1$Write over tens: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $8 \times {\color{blue}1} = 8$Subtract: ${\color{red}9} - 8 = 1$Bring down: $5$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the ones:

| $1$$\color{blue}1$$8$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{9 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 5}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$\color{red}1$$\color{red}5$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$8$$\fbox{7}$ | Divide: ${\color{red}15} \div 8 = {\color{blue}1}\,\text{R}\,7$Write over ones: $\color{blue}1$Multiply: $8 \times {\color{blue}1} = 8$Subtract: ${\color{red}15} - 8 = \fbox{7}$ |
| --- | ---: |

We've gone through all the digits in the number $95$, so the division is done. However, we still have a **remainder** of $\color{blue}7$, so we include this in our final answer.

Therefore,

$$
95 \div 8 = {\color{red}11}\,\text{R}\,{\color{blue}7}
$$

Here, $\color{red}11$ is called the **quotient**." :tutorial/id #uuid "da7b00a0-5a9a-5e5a-acc7-d625c9e3dd99" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1862 :tutorial/title "Dividing Two-Digit Numbers by One-Digit Numbers Using the Standard Algorithm With Remainders"} {:db/id 17592186074952 :tutorial/content "We can use the standard algorithm to divide a three-digit number by a one-digit number. To illustrate, let's divide $468$ by $2$.

We start by writing down the question using long division notation:

| $2$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{4 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 6 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 8}$ |  |
| --- | ---: |

First, we consider the hundreds. How many times does $2$ go into ${\color{red}4}$? It goes in ${\color{blue}2}$ times, and

$$
2\times {\color{blue}2} =4
$$

so there is a remainder of

$$
{\color{red}4} - 4 = 0
$$

We write the ${\color{blue}2}$ above the hundreds, the $4$ at the bottom, and subtract to get the remainder of $0$. Then we bring the tens digit $(6)$ down next to the remainder.

| $\color{blue}2$$2$$\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}4} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 6 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 8}$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$4$$\color{lightgray}\downarrow$$0$$\color{lightgray}6$ | Divide: ${\color{red}4} \div 2 = {\color{blue}2}$Write over hundreds: $\color{blue}2$Multiply: $2 \times {\color{blue}2} = 4$Subtract: ${\color{red}4} - 4 = 0$Bring down: $6$ |
| --- | ---: |

Next, we consider the tens. How many times does $2$ go into ${\color{red}6}$? It goes in ${\color{blue}3}$ times, and

$$
2\times {\color{blue}3} =6
$$

so there is a remainder of

$$
{\color{red}6} - 6 = 0

We write the ${\color{blue}3}$ above the tens, the $6$ at the bottom, and subtract to get the remainder of $0$. Then, we bring the ones digit $(8)$ down next to the remainder.
