\frac{x^{2}}{6} = 1" :db/id 17592186087346}] :answer-field/id #uuid "43395a9a-f3a9-536f-b3ff-c42a92db8e31" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186087341} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45b07bef-5244-588c-9ddc-ae7116c77d2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}=1" :db/id 17592186364448} {:answer/id #uuid "4acaceb8-9337-5d7f-b402-91766ae58363" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{36}=1" :db/id 17592186364449} {:answer/id #uuid "9accd101-1841-5f6d-acf5-e4cfb10226bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}=1" :db/id 17592186364450} {:answer/id #uuid "4ae6cbf5-27d1-5910-b4bc-c5a2676fb501" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}=1" :db/id 17592186364451} {:answer/id #uuid "398cb15c-8bcd-583f-a06a-8a1d47f2bf84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1" :db/id 17592186364452}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364451} :answer-field/id #uuid "777aa002-3a0b-5f6b-b461-590b82ef1b0c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364447}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "da4b3797-7dda-5074-b813-a73affb3ac7b" :question/math-academy-id "q-89294" :question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{\sqrt{6}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{6}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186088881 :tutorial/content "It's possible to write the double angle formula for cosine in two alternative forms.

From the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2{x}+\cos^2{x}=1,$ we obtain $\cos^2{x}=1-\sin^2{x}.$
Substituting this into the double-angle formula for cosine, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡x)-{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives an alternative form of the double-angle formula for cosine. We'll restate it below:

$$
\cos{2x} =1 - 2\sin^2{x}
$$

Similarly, from the same Pythagorean identity, we obtain that $\sin^2{x}=1-\cos^2{x}.$ Substituting into the double-angle formula for cosine, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is another alternative form of the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2{x}-1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5da93916-34c4-5c5a-806c-82bae4dc1e02" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2639 :tutorial/title "Alternative Forms of the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine"} {:db/id 17592186088895 :tutorial/content "Given a $2 \times 2$ matrix

<div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$A =\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>

the **inverse** of $A$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9694c9ae-0d23-54a2-a458-b9c2262e4fba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3045 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186088916 :tutorial/content "When we add a complex number and its conjugate, the result is always twice the real part of the complex number. That is to say,

$$
z + \overline{z} = 2\operatorname{Re}(z),
$$

where $\operatorname{Re}(z)$ is the real part of $z.$

For example, suppose we have a complex number $z = 3+4\textrm{i}.$ To obtain the conjugate, we just flip the sign of the imaginary part and get $\overline{z} = 3 - 4 \textrm{i}.$

Now, adding $z$ and its conjugate $\overline{z},$ we find that the real part $(3)$ is doubled while the imaginary part $(4)$ is canceled out:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+\overset{―}{z} & =(3+4\text{i})+(3-4\text{i}) \\  & =(3+3)+(4\text{i}-4\text{i}) \\  & =6+0\text{i} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

This result holds in general. For any complex number $z=x+\textrm{i}y,$ the conjugate is $\overline{z} = x-\textrm{i}y,$ and when we add, we find that the real part $(x)$ is doubled while the imaginary part $(y)$ is canceled out:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+\overset{―}{z} & =(x+\text{i}y)+(x-\text{i}y) \\  & =(x+x)+(\text{i}y-\text{i}y) \\  & =2x+\text{i}0 \\  & =2x \\  & =2Re(z).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aa576d65-023e-5ad0-9cc8-fff8c2b730f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3425 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186088917 :tutorial/content "When we multiply a complex number and its conjugate, the result is always the sum of squares of the real part and the imaginary part. That is to say,

$$
z\overline{z} = x^2 + y^2 = (\operatorname{Re}(z))^2 + (\operatorname{Im}(z))^2.
$$

For example, suppose we have a complex number $z=3+4\textrm{i}.$  To obtain the conjugate, we just flip the sign of the imaginary part and get $\overline{z} = 3 - 4 \textrm{i}.$

Now, multiplying $z$ and its conjugate $\overline{z},$ we find that the result is the sum of squares of the real part $(3^2=9)$ and the imaginary part $(4^2=16)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\overset{―}{z} & =(3+4\text{i})(3-4\text{i}) \\  & ={3}^{2}-3(4\text{i})+3(4\text{i})-{4}^{2}{\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =9-12\text{i}+12\text{i}-16(-1) \\  & =9+16 \\  & =25\end{aligned}
$$

This result holds in general. For any complex number $z=x+\textrm{i}y,$ the conjugate is $\overline{z} = x-\textrm{i}y,$ and when we multiply, we find that the result is the sum of squares of the real part $(x^2)$ and the imaginary part $(y^2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\overset{―}{z} & =(x+\text{i}y)(x-\text{i}y) \\  & ={x}^{2}-\text{i}xy+\text{i}xy-{\text{i}}^{2}{y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-(-1){y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\  & =(Re(z))^{2}+(Im(z))^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "282ac3b7-1a83-5a26-9532-97ac664356fc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3427 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Product of a Complex Number and its Conjugate"} {:db/id 17592186088973 :tutorial/content "We've been told that the parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin are

$$
x=a\sec{t},\quad y=b\tan{t}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. Can we be sure that these equations do indeed describe a hyperbola?

First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =a\operatorname{sec}⁡t & ⟹ &  & \operatorname{sec}⁡t & =\frac{x}{a}, \\ y & =b\operatorname{tan}⁡t & ⟹ &  & \operatorname{tan}⁡t & =\frac{y}{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}.
$$

Substituting the above into the secant-tangent identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ {\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)}^{2}+1 & ={\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)}^{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the Cartesian equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin. Therefore, the parametric equations do indeed describe a horizontal hyperbola." :tutorial/id #uuid "fb10cbc8-566e-5d0f-82ce-e8d9fb516e6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4633 :tutorial/title "Explanation of the Parametric Equations of Hyperbolas Centered at the Origin"} {:db/id 17592186088988 :tutorial/content "The first few prime numbers are

$$
2,\quad 3, \quad 5, \quad 7, \quad 11, \quad 13, \quad 17, \quad 19, \quad 23, \quad 29, \quad \ldots\,.
$$

Remember that $1$ is *not* a prime number.

A number's **prime factors** are the prime numbers that divide the number with no remainder. 

Let's list the prime factors of $45{:}$

- $2$ is *not* a prime factor of $45$ since dividing $45$ by $2$ gives a remainder of $1. \quad{\color{red}{\times}}$

- $3$ *is* a prime factor of $45$ since $45 \div 3 = 15.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $5$ *is* a prime factor of $45$ since $45 \div 5 = 9.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $7$ is *not* a prime factor of $45$ since dividing $45$ by $7$ gives a remainder of $3. \quad{\color{red}{\times}}$

There are no other prime numbers that divide $45.$ Therefore, the prime factors of $45$ are $3$ and $5.$

We often wish to find a number's prime factors. We'll discuss this more in a future lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "de204ea3-c1d3-5d64-979c-a9285f3da4ca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7959 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186091934 :question/id #uuid "48d7b03b-c991-574a-bf15-8765ca43724b" :question/math-academy-id "e-11113" :question/problem "Let $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T$ be a bivariate normal random vector. The variances of $X_1$ and $X_2$ and their correlation coefficient are given by

$$
\sigma_1^2=9,\qquad \sigma_2^2 = 1, \qquad \rho = \dfrac1{3}.
$$

Given that the joint probability density function of $\mathbf X$ is

$$
f(\mathbf x) = \dfrac1k\,\mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)\right),
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is the mean vector and $\Sigma$ is the corresponding covariance matrix, find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T$ is a bivariate normal vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{pmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{pmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} \\ \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\sigma^2_i = \textrm{Var}[X_i],$ $\sigma_{12} = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2],$ and $\rho$ is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of $\mathbf X$ is

$$
f(\mathbf x) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)
$$

and $|\Sigma|$ denotes the determinant of $\Sigma.$

Using the given values of $\sigma^2_1, \sigma^2_2$, and $\rho,$ our covariance matrix is

$$
\Sigma 
= 

{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}9 & \frac{1}{3} \cdot  \sqrt{9} \cdot  \sqrt{1} \\ \frac{1}{3} \cdot  \sqrt{9} \cdot  \sqrt{1} & 1\end{array} \right]}


=

{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\Sigma| = 9\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 1 = 8.
$$

Substituting this value into our expression for the joint PDF, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{8}}exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi \sqrt{2}}exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $k=4\pi\sqrt 2.$"} {:db/id 17592186091935 :question/id #uuid "90ff4bf9-f8d3-5179-9d02-0e0a46a3cc98" :question/math-academy-id "e-11114" :question/problem "Let $\mathbf{X} = [X_1,X_2]^T$ be a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -3 \\ -3 & 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the distribution of $Y = 3X_1 + X_2 .$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T$ is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y= aX_1 + bX_2
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ Var[Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $\mu_1 = 2$ and $\mu_2 = -1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[3{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}] \\  & =3\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & =3\cdot {\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2} \\  & =3\cdot 2+(-1) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have $\sigma_1^2 = 4, \sigma_2^2 = 7,$ and $\sigma_{12} = \sigma_{21} = -3.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Var[Y] & =Var[3{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}] \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 4+{1}^{2}\cdot 7+2\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot (-3) \\  & =36+7-18 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
Y \sim N(5,25).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186091936 :question/id #uuid "f9e6c722-6017-57b9-9de6-c83c2f14c8c4" :question/math-academy-id "e-11115" :question/problem "Let $\mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2,X_3]^T$ be a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the distribution of $Y = X_1 -2X_2 +4 X_3.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $\mathbf{X} =  [X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k]^T$ is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma,$ then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y= \mathbf c^T \mathbf X = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i X_i
$$

is a normally distributed random variable, where $\mathbf c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and  

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ Var[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, since we wish to know the distribution of $Y = X_1 -2X_2 +4 X_3,$ we have 

$$
\mathbf c = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2 \\ 4\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, for the mean of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu  \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1-4+4 \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the variance of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ 3 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =12-6+56 \\  & =62.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
Y\sim N(1,62).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186091945 :question/id #uuid "cc45cc10-61e3-5cb7-babc-7253a5158c4b" :question/math-academy-id "e-12767" :question/problem "$$
\mathbf{1}_{A}(-1) = 0, \qquad \mathbf{1}_{B}(-1) = 1
$$

Given the values of the indicator functions of the sets $A$ and $B,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $\mathbf{1}_{A \,\cup\, B}\,(-1) = 1$

II. $\mathbf{1}_{A \,\cup\, B}\,(-1) = 0$

III. $-1 \in A \cup B$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the indicator functions of $\overline{A},$ $A \cap B,$ and $A \cup B$ have the following properties:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(x) & =1-{1}_{A}(x) \\ {1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(x) & =min\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\} \\ {1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(x) & =max\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\}\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true while statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(-1) & =max\{{1}_{A}(-1),{1}_{B}(-1)\} \\  & =max\{0,1\} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $\mathbf{1}_{A \,\cup\, B}\,(-1) = 1,$ we conclude that $-1$ belongs to $A \cup B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186091946 :question/id #uuid "5ae8b304-5ce3-5520-8893-92a02784155d" :question/math-academy-id "e-1316" :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

I. $(5x^2-10x^3) \div (5x)$

II. $(1-x^3) \div (x^3)$

III. $(2x^5) \cdot (-x^3-7)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that polynomials have the following closure properties:

- Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. This means that the sum, difference, and product of two polynomials is *always* a polynomial.

- Polynomials are *not* closed under division. This means that the quotient of two polynomials is *not* always a polynomial.

With that in mind, let's examine our expressions in turn.

- Expression I is a polynomial. Even though polynomials are *not* closed under division, the quotient of these two polynomials results in a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3})÷(5x) & =\frac{5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3}}{5x} \\  & =\frac{5x(x-2{x}^{2})}{5x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{5x}(x-2{x}^{2})}{\cancel{5x}} \\  & =x-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Expression II is *not* a polynomial. Carrying out the division, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

- Expression III is a polynomial. It's a product of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186092026 :question/id #uuid "d32f2604-fc3f-5e80-8085-483e6fd9a3ad" :question/math-academy-id "e-4521" :question/problem "Solve the following system of linear equations using matrices:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3y+x+z &=0 \\ z+4y-5 &=2 \\ 1+2x-y &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we organize the system so that the variables are in the correct order and every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y+z &=0 \\ 0x+4y+z &=7 \\ 2x-y+0z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:



$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}
$$



Now, the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$ So, we compute $A^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1*: Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)-3(-2)+(-8) \\  & =1+6-8 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2*: Compute the matrix of minors.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & -7 \\ -1 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3*:  Find the matrix of cofactors.



$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -8 \\ -1 & -2 & 7 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$



*Step 4*: Transpose the matrix of cofactors.



$$
C^T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & -1 \\ -8 & 7 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$



*Step 5*: Apply the inverse matrix formula.



$$
A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det (A)}C^T=\dfrac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & -1 \\ -8 & 7 & 4\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & -7 & -4\end{bmatrix} .
$$



Finally, we can calculate the solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & -7 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 10 \\ -33\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3,$ $y=10,$ $z=-33.$"} {:db/id 17592186092037 :question/id #uuid "667cc169-01b1-5cd1-88ae-6a36335e1daf" :question/math-academy-id "e-5274" :question/problem "Simplify $\left[3\,\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]^3$." :question/worked-solution "We use the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}
[rcis(θ)]^{n} &= r^{n}cis(nθ)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $n=3$, $r=3$, and

$$
\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}
$$

Substituting in these values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
[3cis\left(\frac{π}{4}\right)]^{3} &= 3^{3}cis(3 \cdot \frac{π}{4}) = 27cis\left(\frac{3π}{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
r\,\textrm{cis}(\theta) = r \left[ \cos (\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(\theta) \right]
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
27cis\left(\frac{3π}{4}\right) &= 27[\cos \left(\frac{3π}{4}\right) + \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{3π}{4}\right)] \\
&= 27(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \textrm{i}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\
&=-\frac{27\sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{27\sqrt{2}}{2}\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092072 :question/id #uuid "3e096041-22f8-5b7e-88d7-eca10203a379" :question/math-academy-id "e-5470" :question/problem "![](images/e8/e8ff769df4089e6ed9a47d56d7317acf41b8aef6a255abc705c0e7ec31a446ea.png)

Consider the shaded region $D$ shown above. What is the area of the image of $D$ under the action of the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with the standard matrix $T,$ given below?
$$
T =
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}4 & 2 \\ - 1 & 2\end{array} \right]}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any linear transformation $\mathbf{T},$ we have the following connection between the area of $D$ and the area of the image $\mathbf{T}(D)$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{Area}(\mathbf{T}(D)) = |\det(T)| \cdot \text{Area}(D)
$$

From the diagram, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 6.
$$

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we get 

$$
\det(T) = 4 \cdot 2 -  2 \cdot (-1) = 10.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(D)) & =|det(T)|\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =|\,10\,|\cdot 6 \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092073 :question/id #uuid "e0f036c5-c27d-5a0e-aeb1-cb7c99b49691" :question/math-academy-id "e-5471" :question/problem "A triangle $D$ has vertices $(1,1)$, $(4,5),$ and $(-2,1).$ What is the area of the image of $D$ under the action of the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with the standard matrix $T,$ given below?
$$
T =
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 7 & 5 \\ - 2 & 3\end{array} \right]}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region:

![](images/ee/ee8f0cf16983d87fa505303ed6372a3f389518d05b3e13f2e9e2121038792b84.png)

Recall that for any linear transformation $\mathbf{T},$ we have the following connection between the area of $D$ and the area of the image $\mathbf{T}(D)$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{Area}(\mathbf{T}(D)) = |\det(T)| \cdot \text{Area}(D)
$$

From the diagram, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 6.
$$

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we get 

$$
\det(T) = (-7) \cdot 3 -  5 \cdot (-2) = -11.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(D)) & =|det(T)|\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =|-11|\cdot 6 \\  & =66.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092074 :question/id #uuid "aebe3048-cc5b-5340-a15e-d577ae2ee72a" :question/math-academy-id "e-5479" :question/problem "Find the characteristic equation of the matrix 
$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{array} \right]}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the matrix $\, A-\lambda I\mathbin{:}$
﻿﻿﻿$A - \lambda I = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}2 - \lambda  & 4 \\ 3 & 2 - \lambda \end{array} \right]}.$

Then, the characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4\cdot 3 & =0 \\ 4-4\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -8 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092075 :question/id #uuid "55e695b2-4581-5ba7-9604-506234b88323" :question/math-academy-id "e-5480" :question/problem "Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
$$
B= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{array} \right]}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $B-\lambda I\mathbin{:}$
$$
B - \lambda I = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}4 - \lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 4 - \lambda \end{array} \right]}
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $\det(B-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-0\cdot 0 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix $B$ has only one eigenvalue $\lambda=4,$ which is a double root of the characteristic equation. 

**Note:** We also say that $\lambda=4$ has an **algebraic multiplicity** of $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186092076 :question/id #uuid "a42d0af8-869c-5c2a-8182-22b14b9546e2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5481" :question/problem "Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix $A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}10 & 3 \\ 6 & 7\end{array} \right]}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $A - \lambda I\mathbin{:}$
﻿﻿$A - \lambda I = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}10 - \lambda  & 3 \\ 6 & 7 - \lambda \end{array} \right]}$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}10-\lambda  & 3 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(7-\lambda )-3\cdot 6 & =0 \\ 70-7\lambda -10\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-18 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-17\lambda +52 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{17\pm \sqrt{(-17)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 52}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{17\pm \sqrt{81}}{2} \\  & =\frac{17\pm 9}{2} \\  & =13,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda=13$ and $\lambda=4.$"} {:db/id 17592186092077 :question/id #uuid "9e40836e-18e9-5df6-a930-05875b920335" :question/math-academy-id "e-5482" :question/problem "Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix $A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}3 & 0 \\ 9 & - 2 \sqrt{3}\end{array} \right]}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $A - \lambda I \mathbin{:}$
﻿﻿﻿$A - \lambda I = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}3 - \lambda  & 0 \\ 9 & - 2 \sqrt{3} - \lambda \end{array} \right]}$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $\det (A - \lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 9 & -2\sqrt{3}-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(-2\sqrt{3}-\lambda )-9\cdot 0 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda +2\sqrt{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda={\color{red}3}$ and $\lambda={\color{blue}-2\sqrt{3}}.$

If we look again at the matrix $\,A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}3} & 0 \\ 9 & {\color{blue}- 2 \sqrt{3}}\end{array} \right]},$
we see that the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. This is true in general: the eigenvalues of a *triangular* or *diagonal* matrix are *always* given by the entries on the main diagonal!

**Watch out!** For a general matrix (which is neither triangular nor diagonal), this might not be the case!"} {:db/id 17592186092082 :question/id #uuid "86835544-a7f1-5be2-99c1-14e39a14f3fd" :question/math-academy-id "e-603" :question/problem "Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].
$$

![](images/15/15d185178bf8882f837c19361d630c0e537e145ca2337cad4655677255d0348a.png)" :question/worked-solution "Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092089 :question/id #uuid "0d1dcc59-e7af-5a86-87ba-aa7ee1b23767" :question/math-academy-id "e-632" :question/problem "Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = \cos(3\theta)$ and the lines $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](images/35/350a721c254dab3a8acb2ae54ca5be0bcde6ab036e6936939194c57ae55fe4ff.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = \cos(3\theta),$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}((\frac{\pi }{6}-\left(-\frac{\pi }{6}\right))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092090 :question/id #uuid "6040d180-ed1d-52b8-809c-b5820352d3d8" :question/math-academy-id "e-633" :question/problem "Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 1+2\cos\theta$ for $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3},
$$ as shown below.

![](images/6b/6bfa0990b560bcb09f2a9eb0b9542296f2a8f1c196b6740702e81c59941d66c5.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092091 :question/id #uuid "8a885f78-0028-5b6e-80e6-1215f5d934a2" :question/math-academy-id "e-639" :question/problem "Find the **total** area of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=2\cos(2\theta)$ and $r=1,$ as shown below.

![](images/7c/7c023033b4d3e0fa6ea5a2d9866688e360b759fba6aa0a5dd6241e148d7b093d.png)" :question/worked-solution "Consider the rightmost pair of petals. First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $2\theta \in [-\pi,\pi]$:

$$
2\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{\pi}{3} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta= -\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/1d/1dc9ce9add3d7135f69c92590ebde003d4e5ee31446d6202222ac890e2f42a9c.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=1,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2\cos(2\theta).$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta,
$$

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}((2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}-{1}^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(4{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )-1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))-1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{6}-\left(-\frac{\pi }{6}\right))+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{2\pi }{3}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4{A}_{1}=4(\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4})=\frac{2\pi }{3}+\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092092 :question/id #uuid "c30d91c2-ee63-5b20-ab39-6d356f711fd8" :question/math-academy-id "e-640" :question/problem "Find the shaded area that lies between the polar curves $r=\sin\theta$ and $r=2\sin\theta,$ as shown below.

![](images/23/2389273b09df3e9bc9262a2daed848fbd518707e683e5d06a8dd0217766036bb.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in \left[0,\pi\right]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\theta = 0, \pi
$$

To determine the inner function and the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/4c/4ce437c0d6b1f196269c5c1e56e687a6dca21fd407834dce20bfa7ac76298002.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=\sin\theta,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2\sin\theta.$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta,
$$

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=0, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\pi.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }((2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\theta -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(\pi -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{2})-(0-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2})] \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092093 :question/id #uuid "57034318-5a6e-53f6-a8d3-ae8c61692947" :question/math-academy-id "e-641" :question/problem "![](images/0b/0bb9e5e7315d4bcd5fc21700fdd2597f6d9b585a109145de53c6f94e9530eabf.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above)." :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right)}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092105 :question/id #uuid "a2d8dca5-a0f3-5b6f-81f5-4eea46ee70d8" :question/math-academy-id "e-6822" :question/problem "![](images/d7/d7b39805131dc562e233d49a84f69d30e80ca29cb9443012032d18fdb4512054.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta$ for $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},
$$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ this gives 

$$

Let $y = \sinh{\left(x^2\right)}.$
Since $x \geq 0,$ we have $y \geq 0.$

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
x = \sinh{\left(y^2\right)},
$$

where $x\in[0,\infty)$ and $y\in[0,\infty).$

Next, we apply the definition of $\sinh x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{{y}^{2}}-{e}^{-{y}^{2}}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{{y}^{2}}-{e}^{-{y}^{2}} \\ 2x{e}^{{y}^{2}} & ={e}^{2{y}^{2}}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{y}^{2}}-2x{e}^{{y}^{2}}-1 & =0 \\ {({e}^{{y}^{2}})}^{2}-2x({e}^{{y}^{2}})-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y = e^{y^2}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY-1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ {e}^{{y}^{2}} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $e^{y^2} >0$ for all real $y,$ and $x -\sqrt{x^2+1} <0,$ we must select the positive branch:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{y}^{2}} & =x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{y}^{2}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ {y}^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we require $y\ge 0,$ we select the positive solution. Therefore,

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092471 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "60627aba-89ef-53b6-b4ce-ca7854856bfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186236430} {:answer/id #uuid "70edbcb1-0834-5f95-9e7a-268c0a3c7bca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186236535} {:answer/id #uuid "806bb986-60b0-52f0-9e7d-fe440e12d7b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186236617} {:answer/id #uuid "d998f6fb-b8bd-532a-8961-d0fc2000cb68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186237195} {:answer/id #uuid "da1538df-e67c-5454-aadf-6bd6796416e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186237201}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186237201} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb257275-f2f7-5467-9be9-cb2bc1b74739" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186237704}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dcf46b6f-f5d9-5eec-afdf-9ca4614f945b" :question/math-academy-id "q-10255" :question/problem "![](images/ac/ac040bc2c3eb943f947f34602c7c03e90f18e129a0fa7749d8ae60faaab12f71.png)

$$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186092516 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9cbcb05c-0d49-5cbd-80eb-6b804f107249" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$λ = \sqrt{3}$ $$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3}-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & 2-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{3}-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (\sqrt{3}-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-0\cdot 4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -\sqrt{3})(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =\sqrt{3}$ and $\lambda =2.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are the entries on the main diagonal."} {:db/id 17592186092554 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d0210349-d658-56bd-8f80-e31fccac3a60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186089496} {:answer/id #uuid "e1eb60db-f954-5877-a166-eaa4edacda1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186089497} {:answer/id #uuid "0f0c2601-d71d-5e69-8744-62171093b7de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186089498} {:answer/id #uuid "2f9c787c-b254-506e-a140-14df70ac0529" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186089499} {:answer/id #uuid "39bbda71-17a5-5873-b28b-20983276c6e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186089500}] :answer-field/id #uuid "0f0b6a73-9b4a-5a58-b5c8-ca19e491d602" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186089495}] :question/id #uuid "f96cf055-993b-5aae-b24a-69010655c966" :question/math-academy-id "q-141204" :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ Var[Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=0$ and ${\mu }_{2}=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]-2\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & ={\mu }_{1}-2\cdot {\mu }_{2} \\  & =0-2\cdot (1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=1,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Var[Y] & =Var[{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2}] \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 1+(-2)^{2}\cdot 4+2\cdot 1\cdot (-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =1+16-4 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
Y∼N(-2,13).

from $t=-3$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?" :question/worked-solution "To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}

The variances of ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ and their covariance are given by

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{2}=10,\,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=5,\,{\sigma }_{12}=5.
$$

Given that the joint probability density function of $X$ is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{k}\,exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )),
$$

where $\mu $ is the mean vector and $Σ$ is the corresponding covariance matrix, find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ is a bivariate normal vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{pmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{pmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} \\ \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\sigma }_{i}^{2}=\text{Var}[{X}_{i}],$ ${\sigma }_{12}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}],$ and $\rho $ is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of $X$ is

$$
f({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{|Σ|}}exp(-\frac{1}{2}(X-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(X-\mu ))
$$

and $|Σ|$ denotes the determinant of $Σ.$

Using the given values of ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}$, and ${\sigma }_{12},$ our covariance matrix is

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}10 & 5 \\ 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|Σ|=10\cdot 5-5\cdot 5=25.
$$

Substituting this value into our expression for the joint PDF, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{25}}exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )) \\  & =\frac{1}{10\pi }exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $k=10\pi .$"} {:db/id 17592186092580 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a17a8449-31bb-525a-8ca5-1e66b4a439fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1711" :db/id 17592186089652} {:answer/id #uuid "a49337cb-0f46-5c90-84d8-7f669ba7f29b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1762" :db/id 17592186089653} {:answer/id #uuid "d019c2f7-49d1-571b-ac68-b7db432075f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1977" :db/id 17592186089654} {:answer/id #uuid "de43eab0-c4d8-5a9d-b725-ecc7339189c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2033" :db/id 17592186089655} {:answer/id #uuid "4eaee5a4-a5b3-5342-a3a6-6a78faf919f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2005" :db/id 17592186089656}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186089655} :answer-field/id #uuid "d5efdcd4-17d6-5391-871c-f2a692148bfc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186089651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "89c577b9-8c2b-5e60-9161-7d08d52dcc46" :question/math-academy-id "q-159694" :question/problem "Let $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ be a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ$ given by

" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ Var[Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=0$ and ${\mu }_{2}=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]-2\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & ={\mu }_{1}-2\cdot {\mu }_{2} \\  & =0-2\cdot (1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=1,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Var[Y] & =Var[{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2}] \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 1+(-2)^{2}\cdot 4+2\cdot 1\cdot (-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =1+16-4 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(-2,13).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(Y\ge 1).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 1) & =P(Z\ge \frac{1-(-2)}{\sqrt{13}}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.832)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 0.83) & =1-P(Z<0.83) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.83) \\  & =1-Φ(0.83)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(0.83)=0.7967.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 0.83) & =1-Φ(0.83) \\  & =1-0.7967 \\  & =0.2033.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{k}]^{T}$ is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y={c}^{T}X={\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{c}_{i}{X}_{i}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable, where $c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and  

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ Var[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, since we wish to know the distribution of $Y={X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}-{X}_{3},$ we have 

$$
c=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, for the mean of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu  \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3+2-2 \\  & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the variance of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3+10-1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(3,12).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(Y<1).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<1) & =P(Z<\frac{1-3}{\sqrt{12}}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.58)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z<-0.58) & =P(Z\le -0.58) \\  & =Φ(-0.58).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(0.58)=0.7190.
$$

By the symmetry of the normal distribution, we have

$$
Φ(-0.58)=1-Φ(0.58)=1-0.7190=0.2810.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z<-0.58)=0.2810.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(Y<1)=0.2810.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092602 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d280c1f-3e76-55d8-ac14-ba38ed573031" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the indicator functions of $\overset{―}{A},$ $A\cap B,$ and $A\cup B$ have the following properties:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(x) & =1-{1}_{A}(x) \\ {1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(x) & =min\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\} \\ {1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(x) & =max\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\}\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(5)=1$ is false while statement ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(5)=0$ is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(5) & =min\{{1}_{A}(5),{1}_{B}(5)\} \\  & =min\{1,0\} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement $5\in A\cap B$ is false. Since ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(5)=0,$ we conclude that $5$ does not belong to $A\cap B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(5)=0$ only."} {:db/id 17592186092604 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9d76cebc-b6fb-5524-8283-b87a8706d0a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186089796} {:answer/id #uuid "a035904c-4fe1-5a9f-a9bf-e49750aa30b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186089797} {:answer/id #uuid "f97d5917-25f1-5529-9b0f-beee8799d9a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186089798} {:answer/id #uuid "48009762-6e64-51c1-8c34-e8d675fca580" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186089799} {:answer/id #uuid "678c699c-69d3-50d3-949b-5005fc07d7cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186089800}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186089797} :answer-field/id #uuid "88da4f35-85b0-53f0-a65f-db9edf474b77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186089795}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bab9e63e-a883-5b00-876f-108808a6cc8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-172723" :question/problem "$$

III. $5\in A\cup B$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the indicator functions of $\overset{―}{A},$ $A\cap B,$ and $A\cup B$ have the following properties:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(x) & =1-{1}_{A}(x) \\ {1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(x) & =min\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\} \\ {1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(x) & =max\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\}\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true while statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(5) & =max\{{1}_{A}(5),{1}_{B}(5)\} \\  & =max\{1,0\} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since ${1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(5)=1,$ we conclude that $5$ belongs to $A\cup B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186092628 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6b4da550-43d1-5bf0-ba07-2d9c8866fa45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi -8}{2}" :db/id 17592186528557} {:answer/id #uuid "87cb5c61-72c1-5207-ac68-6c4fc40a404e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi +8}{2}" :db/id 17592186528625} {:answer/id #uuid "9c7ba2fb-9f38-56bc-8fe5-e96e6dbabc3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi +8}{4}" :db/id 17592186528675} {:answer/id #uuid "a23714c3-4f78-5ba1-a107-d1e73692eea4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi +4}{2}" :db/id 17592186528692} {:answer/id #uuid "f974103f-b624-52cf-acc4-f3366c464e19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186528919}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186528557} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d48976e-ecd9-52fe-8371-edaabd05c065" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186090051}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb2c5d25-e3ba-5c5d-9450-482e68e4a749" :question/math-academy-id "q-20640" :question/problem "![](images/4a/4a83949bcdf4ed8d99cac451d6db21986c24819d1601578890f86fe3df99666a.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092689 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e42bea0-ae31-5c53-973d-aa17ac450933" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -4=0" :db/id 17592186321378} {:answer/id #uuid "3c9bdffb-21f8-5d69-a0bd-17fe65627150" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4=0" :db/id 17592186321615} {:answer/id #uuid "3f87dd55-fd67-54f3-a30e-392aed0248a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +9=0" :db/id 17592186321646} {:answer/id #uuid "ac110cfb-d9fa-56d7-95de-4b61052b6737" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\lambda }^{2}-1=0" :db/id 17592186322495} {:answer/id #uuid "f703d3fa-fa27-5c44-95ed-f194c20cdf12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4=0" :db/id 17592186323086}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186323086} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d352f44-669a-5112-9b66-540b684a29de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "21a76447-bb7c-5d72-a771-38739632e899" :question/math-academy-id "q-36758" :question/problem "Find the characteristic equation of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -8 & -6\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}2-\lambda  & 2 \\ -8 & -6-\lambda \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then, the characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 2 \\ -8 & -6-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )-(-8)\cdot 2 & =0 \\ -12-2\lambda +6\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092691 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24a537b1-5dc1-566a-9e74-e2dcfcb05234" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =6$ and $\lambda =10$" :db/id 17592186321430} {:answer/id #uuid "2f09fc12-e77b-5d3a-8bf5-3206a98228e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "There are no real eigenvalues" :db/id 17592186321511} {:answer/id #uuid "8109cdb3-fff2-519d-b607-3ccd4eadccb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =8$ and $\lambda =5$" :db/id 17592186322162} {:answer/id #uuid "aa2951cc-d69d-5205-be76-aee83aade18c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =-6$ and $\lambda =-10$" :db/id 17592186322485} {:answer/id #uuid "da37b8b4-b86c-52be-9edf-4d44daca250f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =8$ (double root)" :db/id 17592186322856}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321511} :answer-field/id #uuid "255562d5-b67b-5f8c-b0e9-9ed67cabbd41" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323241}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f563abe4-0d8d-5d69-9a75-20dcd9079f0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-36776" :question/problem "Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
$$
\displaystyle Q=\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -3 \\ 2 & -10\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $Q-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
Q-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-6-\lambda  & -3 \\ 2 & -10-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(Q-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Q-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-6-\lambda  & -3 \\ 2 & -10-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-10-\lambda )-(-3)\cdot 2 & =0 \\ 60+6\lambda +10\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+16\lambda +66 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the discriminant of the quadratic equation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={16}^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 66 \\  & =256-264 \\  & =-8 \\  & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the characteristic equation does not have real solutions, and therefore, $Q$ does not have real eigenvalues."} {:db/id 17592186092709 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f1c5547-1ac6-53d1-b475-3c1f3a7a7421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186327355} {:answer/id #uuid "cc9bc47f-e4a1-5a48-ad95-9fdc8c30c725" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186328727} {:answer/id #uuid "e561604b-c400-5b31-b7b4-38788bbd36a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186328943} {:answer/id #uuid "ee8db0ff-6f78-5797-8626-bb072f3b6837" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186329018} {:answer/id #uuid "ef36cb4d-9cd4-585e-b2e1-dfd00cf7e9a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186329023}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186327355} :answer-field/id #uuid "b8241441-5d37-5b80-8d02-80f7b14d12b8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186329508}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "be9d95c2-a710-5571-987b-8cd6ddd0d0ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-42449" :question/problem "Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3+z &=0 \\ 5y-1+3x &=2z+1 \\ 3z+2x-1 &=2y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+z &=3 \\ 3x+5y-2z &=2 \\ 2x-2y+3z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-0+\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(15-4)+(-6-10) \\  & =22-16 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 5\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 & 13 & -16 \\ 2 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & -7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -13 & -16 \\ -2 & 4 & 4 \\ -5 & 7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -24 \\ -30\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $x+y+z=4-4-5=-5.$"} {:db/id 17592186092732 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "070b1605-3f0f-5052-807c-9e2da26f1b13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}" :db/id 17592186525221} {:answer/id #uuid "2d8415e7-55ff-5ae3-b4f6-b66c8c1d541d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{(5x-2)}" :db/id 17592186525312} {:answer/id #uuid "4f82f8a5-4d83-5410-bc3d-5d0dbb832acc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{(2x-5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}" :db/id 17592186525407} {:answer/id #uuid "7e998750-c647-5300-8e4d-ccc8bad0a0cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}" :db/id 17592186525520} {:answer/id #uuid "845c0b40-9827-530c-894b-969a75a5872a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}" :db/id 17592186525539}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186525221} :answer-field/id #uuid "80eb6a81-e7b7-57ed-8210-04192f46d9f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186090592}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6612d2f1-5666-54fd-9c5c-1217f3a2dfe0" :question/math-academy-id "q-48008" :question/problem "Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y={log}_{3}⁡(5x-2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$

$$

Which of the following gives the area of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $r=1,$ as shown above?" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the values of $\theta $ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We have two solutions: 

$\,$ $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}$    

To determine the inner function and the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/d8/d802b734480b75e6e8e16f49c84fb4685cbcd6ddbdc33c8c40b29de7dc7c3824.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=1,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$

$\,$ ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\,$ and $\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186092898 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35f2c80a-d585-5a1b-a6cf-4bf7d8d37eb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186355153} {:answer/id #uuid "6a23fbcc-05e8-5db0-8dc8-a17157353f37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186355601} {:answer/id #uuid "762a042f-abf4-5263-a895-2f32e4b8ec08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186355699} {:answer/id #uuid "b878533b-b908-58a8-88a5-cf162499f7f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356281} {:answer/id #uuid "d9883d1d-7aed-598f-b250-adbdcb6374e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186356572}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186355601} :answer-field/id #uuid "06526027-3b2f-5cc0-bb6a-ad2676da0aa0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186356926}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fdc48455-0a40-5b7f-be99-05aa87be4ff6" :question/math-academy-id "q-9294" :question/problem "What is the area scale factor of the linear transformation $T$ that is given by its standard matrix

$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(7-\lambda )-2\cdot 6 & =0 \\ -28-7\lambda +4\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -40 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{(-3)^{2}+4\cdot 1\cdot 40}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{169}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\pm 13}{2} \\  & =8,-5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $A-\lambda I:$

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}3-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+1\cdot 1 & =0 \\ 3-3\lambda -\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
