$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{4}{x{log}_{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{log}_{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|){|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =4{ln}^{2}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101536 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "383be394-a41f-5e0f-b93b-a0ff9878be08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{7}⁡(4x)|+C" :db/id 17592186339635} {:answer/id #uuid "750a3dcf-e361-507f-ad62-9dbb75727d78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡4\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{7}⁡x|+C" :db/id 17592186340176} {:answer/id #uuid "aa31712a-2e4f-527b-a00c-e331135a4450" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡7}{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{7}⁡(4x)|+C" :db/id 17592186340682} {:answer/id #uuid "dc05d22a-2a20-518f-afa3-1ccc9267a967" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\operatorname{ln}⁡7\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{7}⁡({x}^{4})|+C" :db/id 17592186341082} {:answer/id #uuid "e0868377-7786-5248-883a-b568427cad5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡7\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{7}⁡(4x)|+C" :db/id 17592186341122}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341122} :answer-field/id #uuid "aff887c8-fb12-5cba-942f-5f6c84cf518a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341687}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "15940cb6-48bb-51bb-99eb-a693e64f76c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-73659" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x{log}_{7}⁡(4x)}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u={log}_{7}⁡(4x).$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡7}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡7\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{x{log}_{7}⁡(4x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{log}_{7}⁡(4x)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡7\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡7\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡7\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡7\operatorname{ln}⁡|{log}_{7}⁡(4x)|+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101963 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have two vectors $\textbf{u}=\langle 1, 3 \rangle$ and $\textbf{v}=\langle 2,-1 \rangle.$ The parallelogram spanned by $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ is shown in the picture below:

![](images/10/102f72ba6730d1b07ca0d01186a1ff7851954193f00dc74eb7150981844b0222.png)

Now, we construct a new matrix

<div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$M =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>

where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors. Let's find the determinant of $M\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 3 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

It turns out that the absolute value of $\det(M)$ gives the area $A$ of the parallelogram:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|det(M)| \\  & =|-7| \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "90a7caf1-54f7-517e-93cb-98a6d39494ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3014 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186101964 :tutorial/content "Why does the absolute value of the determinant represent the area of the parallelogram? Let's prove this result.

First, let's state the result precisely. Consider two vectors $\textbf{u}=\langle a,b \rangle$ and $\textbf{v}=\langle c,d \rangle.$ The parallelogram spanned by $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ is shown in the picture below:

![](images/3a/3a466fd3c52ea345d80b9ba67ac104efef29bfd7eeed0e4567364c80f3212c0d.png)

We construct a new matrix

<div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$M =\begin{bmatrix}a & c \\ b & d\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>

where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors. Then the absolute value of $\det(M)$ gives the area $A$ of the parallelogram spanned by $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}\mathbin{:}$

$$
A = |\det(M)|
$$

To prove the formula, we use the following picture:

![](images/3d/3da110b114d2038738bd4ef06cb031bb8b66aee062ffc83955dfdaade72584e1.png)

We can compute the area by starting with the area of the outer rectangle, and then subtracting off the area of the smaller triangles and rectangles surrounding the parallelogram:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|(a+c)(b+d)-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}cd-2\cdot ad-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}ab| \\  & =|ab+ad+bc+cd-cd-2ad-ab| \\  & =|bc-ad| \\  & =|ad-bc| \\  & =|det(M)|\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca25b302-10d5-5d18-a10f-0c50af28db94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3015 :tutorial/title "General Rule"} {:db/id 17592186101966 :tutorial/content "When two vectors are parallel, the parallelogram does not exist. So, it has zero area.

![](images/b6/b65c64ccf16764f99c0c30dbf6b37ce7b6254b83496512a5d207dddab095dac7.png)

As a result, the determinant of a matrix whose columns are parallel vectors must also be zero. 

For example, in the diagram above, we have the vectors $\textbf{u} = \left< 1,1 \right>$ and $\textbf{v} = \left< 2,2 \right>.$ Constructing a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors, we have

<div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$M =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>

Indeed, the determinant does come out to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 2-2\cdot 1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ff830819-9cbf-5fb9-852c-f885f8cd6d68" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3173 :tutorial/title "The Case When Two Vectors are Parallel"} {:db/id 17592186102023 :tutorial/content "To divide powers of the same base, we simply *subtract* the exponents. This is known as the **quotient rule for exponents**. For instance, in the expression 

$$
{\color{blue}3}^5 \div {\color{blue}3}^2,
$$

both powers have the same base $({\color{blue}3})$. Therefore, we can simplify this expression by subtracting the exponents:

$$
{\color{blue}3}^5 \div {\color{blue}3}^2 = {\color{blue}3}^{5-2} = {\color{blue}3}^3.
$$

**Note:** The quotient rule for exponents is really just a quicker alternative to the following process:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{5}÷{3}^{2} &= {3}^{3+2}÷{3}^{2} \\ &= {3}^{3}\times \underbrace{{3}^{2}÷{3}^{2}}_{=1} \\ &= {3}^{3}\times 1 \\ &= {3}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4547d33f-6904-539f-b917-599af56aac3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8158 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186102024 :tutorial/content "We can use the quotient rule for exponents with negative exponents too. For example, to simplify $3^{-5}\div 3^{-3},$ we subtract the exponents:

$$
3^{-5} \div 3^{-3} = 3^{-5-(-3)} = 3^{-2}
$$

Now, to evaluate $3^{-2},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(3)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
3^{-2}  = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 =\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b127450f-67ae-5232-a082-2242758636fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8160 :tutorial/title "The Quotient Rule With Negative Exponents"} {:db/id 17592186102029 :tutorial/content "Let's think about how to calculate an integral like $$
\displaystyle \int \dfrac {\ln x} {x} \,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that this integral can be written as

$$
\int \dfrac {\ln x} {x} \,\textrm d x = \int \underbrace{\ln x}_{u} \cdot\overbrace{\dfrac {1} {x}}^{u'} \,\textrm d x.
$$

We've seen integrals like this before, where the integrand consists of a function $u(x)$ multiplied by its derivative $u'(x).$ Such integrals can be solved by substitution.

So, we let $u = \ln x,$ which gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac 1 x\quad   \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac 1 x \,\textrm{d}x={\textrm{d}u}.
$$

 

Therefore, we can calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
       \int \dfrac{\ln x}{x}\, \textrm{d}x 	&=\int \ln x\cdot \dfrac {1} {x} \,\textrm d x \\[5pt]
								& = \int u \, \textrm{d} u \\[5pt]
                                                                &=  \dfrac{1}{2}u^2  +C \\[5pt]   
                                                                &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln^2 x +C\end{aligned}
$$

After solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x+C) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({ln}^{2}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f20c3f56-ce97-548d-a8e0-c4a604acbc18" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8918 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "b358e447-f1de-5dec-828f-1655ba8181dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4 \div (11 \cdot 3)" :db/id 17592186104963} {:answer/id #uuid "d299947e-3567-54b1-a03a-3c24f5b92fbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4^{3} \div 11" :db/id 17592186104964} {:answer/id #uuid "f2351657-92f5-5246-8ba3-edb15734d2ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4 \div (11 + 3)" :db/id 17592186104965} {:answer/id #uuid "18d1c353-4eb5-54c8-b659-08b5f9054710" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4^{3} \div 11^{3}" :db/id 17592186104966} {:answer/id #uuid "53fb43f0-05c0-595d-92b8-4e2380d39a38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4 \div 11^{3}" :db/id 17592186104967} {:db/id 17592186105458 :question/id #uuid "558bc791-1cd4-51fc-9e2c-9efdd063323d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12381" :question/problem "![](images/d8/d8675cb0c59ba915cefe4b0bbe539f1e7e38b5a3ac2fae4bd2bb25e4de96e116.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} x^2y \: \textrm{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\sqrt2x-y$ and whose domain is a semicircle of radius $1$ centered at $O$ in the upper-half plane, as shown above." :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sqrt2x-y) = \sqrt2,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sqrt2x-y) = -1.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{1+(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,[\frac{{r}^{5}}{5}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{[-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105573 :question/id #uuid "625c532a-d455-5b15-880d-e9fc5ae8ee72" :question/math-academy-id "e-374" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle\int \left(\dfrac 2 x\right)\, \textrm{d} x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $2$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\dfrac 1 x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105574 :question/id #uuid "9c57c69e-efa2-5e82-992c-53570e61af09" :question/math-academy-id "e-375" :question/problem "Find the integral of $\dfrac 1 {2x} + 3x$ with respect to $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{2x}+3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x+\int 3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}ln⁡|x|+3\cdot \frac{{x}^{1+1}}{1+1}+C \\  & =\frac{ln⁡|x|}{2}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105575 :question/id #uuid "bf47e35e-da86-5f88-b1e7-0cc731c37b31" :question/math-academy-id "e-376" :question/problem "What is the antiderivative of $\dfrac {3+2x} {x} ?$" :question/worked-solution "We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =3 \ln K$ where $K$ is some other constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+3ln⁡K \\  & =3ln⁡(K|x|)+2x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105580 :question/id #uuid "b18540cc-5822-5620-a36f-60cfbbf3196b" :question/math-academy-id "e-4255" :question/problem "Find $$
\displaystyle \lim_{x \to 4}\log_2 (x+4) .
$$" :question/worked-solution "The function $\log_2 (x+4)$ is defined for $x>-4,$ so the limit as $x \to 4$ exists.

To find this limit, we substitute $x=4$ into the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 4}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4) & ={log}_{2}⁡(4+4) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(8) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{3}) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105646 :question/id #uuid "af255938-10ff-5169-9c5d-eac817354465" :question/math-academy-id "e-635" :question/problem "Find the integral expression corresponding to the area of the first petal of the polar curve $r = \sin(5\theta),$ represented by the shaded region shown below.

![](images/66/66062568cedc1b46822dd7e0e53779482f1923d621b47d29f38141ff770b4498.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta) = \sin(5\theta)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sin(5\theta) = 0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta\in[0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
5\theta = 0, \pi \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{5}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right].$  Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105684 :question/id #uuid "ec8ac943-1880-5f2a-81c3-35c136126ec1" :question/math-academy-id "e-8328" :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

Find the derivative of $y = 3\tanh{x}- \sinh{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic hyperbolic functions:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \sinh x ) = \cosh x,
\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \cosh x ) = \sinh x,
\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \tanh x ) = \sech^2 x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-\operatorname{sinh}⁡x) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x) \\  & =3{sech}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105685 :question/id #uuid "3dcfc1f2-40ee-54b4-a937-0e101c7238d4" :question/math-academy-id "e-8329" :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

Find the derivative of $f(x) = 2x\tanh{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}

Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = 2x$ and $v(x)=\tanh x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(2x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{tanh}⁡x+2x\cdot (\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)^{′} \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{tanh}⁡x+2x\cdot {sech}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+2x{sech}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+x{sech}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105686 :question/id #uuid "1da70111-4e82-5fe4-b4be-08d0cc6f1110" :question/math-academy-id "e-8330" :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}

\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{w}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{3})^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cosh}⁡x-{x}^{3}\cdot (\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)^{′}}{(\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cosh}⁡x-{x}^{3}\cdot \operatorname{sinh}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(3\operatorname{cosh}⁡x-x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x)}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

Find the derivative of $f(x) = \cosh{\sqrt x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f = \cosh g, \qquad g = \sqrt x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g}  = \sinh g,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡g\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sinh}⁡\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186105690 :question/id #uuid "3f355cb7-222f-5992-a212-f1b86ae37ada" :question/math-academy-id "e-9541" :question/problem "Find the interval for $\theta$ corresponding to the first petal of the polar curve $r = \sqrt{2}\cos(6\theta),$ represented by the shaded region shown below.

![](images/9e/9e401186103f1cb3b060b99037bf5af07e873c191324759627275d77d235688c.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta) = \sqrt{2}\cos(6\theta)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sqrt{2}\cos(6\theta) = 0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta$ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $6\theta\in[-\pi,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
6\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{12},\dfrac{\pi}{12}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $$
\displaystyle \theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{12},\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right].
$$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\int_{-\pi/12}^{\pi/12} \cos^2(6\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106037 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04aaf6f0-1ada-5467-bb53-d81bc7503a1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544097} {:answer/id #uuid "4e6a6ef5-246a-53a2-81a7-26459da54ef2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡(3+\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544256} {:answer/id #uuid "55c8f95e-9be1-5a02-b4e5-0870aeadb069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544275} {:answer/id #uuid "66fe0a64-caf0-5d4e-a637-a3c583daff6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544310} {:answer/id #uuid "6a25df31-0140-584d-8f5b-d560aebe68ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544317}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544097} :answer-field/id #uuid "57276f9e-09b6-5a62-a9d8-da3b98983001" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186102108}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a6c70642-adfc-517d-8652-a26cc7fbca82" :question/math-academy-id "q-124423" :question/problem "![](images/1c/1c296052cfe60b35b326029afa1efb610ce32e4e2fb3ae0d63f24e437c3bbfb2.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=2x-y$ and whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-y)=2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-y)=-1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{1+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{6}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =8\sqrt{6}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106064 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "181d1c26-e67d-51c2-a26a-430f785d6acb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186275701} {:answer/id #uuid "28969ccb-d093-57d3-b212-4874bada94e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186275844} {:answer/id #uuid "2ba05209-d34b-5868-9786-58e2ff4e93bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186275874} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2683e3-eb37-586e-9160-3302e36bbab0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186277310} {:answer/id #uuid "e45df712-ce3b-5b93-9b2c-9398a0154cf8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186277472}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275701} :answer-field/id #uuid "ca7cbc3f-0579-5978-bcda-87ea12ce82c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186278081}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1a32ff2f-f5fc-57a4-9ce0-9a59d7c231d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161355" :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

where $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)$ for $0\le x\le \pi $ and $-x\le y\le x.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y),
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\sqrt{1+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y))^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}}\cancel{\sqrt{1+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y))^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-x}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=-x}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106067 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50272988-b890-53f6-a6a1-98aa8ded5b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A rectangle" :db/id 17592186279324} {:answer/id #uuid "622fb80d-5fba-5d31-9969-daf4c626a166" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186279483} {:answer/id #uuid "ae1c8d24-5284-5c7d-95c5-1d06ad681c2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point, different from the origin" :db/id 17592186280134} {:answer/id #uuid "c71bb996-cc27-596e-bd5d-bc10e4c47114" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186280337} {:answer/id #uuid "fb282045-7ab5-5935-b512-2d49501f3d31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The origin $O$ of the coordinate system" :db/id 17592186280792}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279483} :answer-field/id #uuid "eaa2889d-b25a-5184-a3d7-273fb01be88f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281252}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6dc04420-7edf-5061-a2f1-81e1e58efd27" :question/math-academy-id "q-162145" :question/problem "![](images/e2/e2ab6906100a96a123b4b1520613f1e38fe2c7e77af390a8efe0596a2861727d.png)

$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-3)-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. Therefore, the image of the triangle under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} {:db/id 17592186106068 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e72b8eba-d97d-557f-a8cb-b177b5a694e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The origin $O$ of the coordinate system" :db/id 17592186401317} {:answer/id #uuid "239808c3-6662-5144-b216-bf28876d8c30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A rectangle" :db/id 17592186401318} {:answer/id #uuid "d95c8151-cc29-5467-9bd0-4f7145939834" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186401319} {:answer/id #uuid "a539e88c-cfb9-5231-b8f6-481fa85848fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186401320} {:answer/id #uuid "ace8a67a-e74f-5f27-9582-9a2b3428a829" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point, different from the origin" :db/id 17592186401321}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401317} :answer-field/id #uuid "3dd41be4-e0dd-5cb0-830a-bc68816c31ff" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401316}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ba678a53-c013-5d44-b391-2d5cc0a9cc96" :question/math-academy-id "q-162150" :question/problem "![](images/e2/e2ab6906100a96a123b4b1520613f1e38fe2c7e77af390a8efe0596a2861727d.png)

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1\cdot 1-0\cdot 1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a nonsingular matrix. Therefore, the image of our object under the action of  $T$ is a quadrilateral."} {:db/id 17592186106148 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "40c51311-8856-5758-9682-9586a5a3a274" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544232} {:answer/id #uuid "990dde5b-5c60-56f9-aa59-5fb12862070a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544420} {:answer/id #uuid "cb36aeac-bf37-5bf6-bcca-5eac16ae3089" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544518} {:answer/id #uuid "ce96ff87-2f38-5ce1-a84d-662458a4201e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544526} {:answer/id #uuid "f213dbd7-8a94-5e4a-8f52-24a730f798a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544612}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544612} :answer-field/id #uuid "d21499a7-d8b9-5197-a6bf-e3d9bd7a4181" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186102764}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "db057c50-119e-5372-a829-3c2e39e59b9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-20905" :question/problem "![](images/01/01a371be4c5a555b0d3790431111468acfed1471d16c4c4c305bcfe311ce3576.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta \in [0,2\pi ):$

$$
3\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{3}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{3}].$ Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106366 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5ccfd8a7-5c3e-5d8f-b503-a84e866aac9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "ln⁡|x|+9x+C" :db/id 17592186330778} {:answer/id #uuid "83b153b7-2aaa-5823-8b5c-ce9f1a4bbc39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}ln⁡|x|+C" :db/id 17592186331120} {:answer/id #uuid "b1b36a3c-956d-543f-8446-44905d2a0d08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9ln⁡|x|+C" :db/id 17592186331522} {:answer/id #uuid "d02eee89-c918-5d7b-8fe1-0d3c0333afbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "ln⁡(9+x)+C" :db/id 17592186331795} {:answer/id #uuid "e0332c7a-e538-5540-b5ef-e59e8a3977b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "ln⁡(9-x)+C" :db/id 17592186331930}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186331120} :answer-field/id #uuid "aecf8e36-3fbd-5edb-aa3b-f4cafc82e67e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332505}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0721a79b-46f6-56dc-93df-e0a639013e16" :question/math-academy-id "q-49097" :question/problem "Calculate $$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)={sech}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡x) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x)+3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡x) \\  & =2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106539 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b637c9d-91e6-5581-9efa-bec60883d4fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x-x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)}{2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}" :db/id 17592186513649} {:answer/id #uuid "9c2611e4-4e0c-5724-b6ea-f82a8121df8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x-x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}" :db/id 17592186513936} {:answer/id #uuid "cdffa413-16d4-5eb6-ad55-dfdc472ea585" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x-x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}" :db/id 17592186514069} {:answer/id #uuid "d8e40cb5-f377-55c4-ae84-c4ae98fa80a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x-x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x)}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}" :db/id 17592186514100} {:answer/id #uuid "fdf59cbd-7de4-59b2-a619-f048af40fe43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x-x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x)}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}" :db/id 17592186514201}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186514069} :answer-field/id #uuid "b1a5871c-e17d-5053-ab0d-b3a1c9839a97" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186105382}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "539990c8-b61b-5bae-b1f8-037c34589599" :question/math-academy-id "q-95235" :question/problem "Find the derivative of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.$" :question/worked-solution "In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-14\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) \\  & =-14\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) \\  & =-14{sech}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106543 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "61917980-9a7b-5ded-8bc9-fd9f14dfd212" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12{cosh}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186513796} {:answer/id #uuid "9517511c-9bba-5b13-ac76-a5fbb5664726" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12{sinh}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x" :db/id 17592186513918} {:answer/id #uuid "c9ea6e59-85b4-5444-807e-a267c4b16631" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\operatorname{sinh}⁡x{cosh}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186514060} {:answer/id #uuid "e0e529d4-29ad-5e2d-a3bb-7cec86152a0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{sinh}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x" :db/id 17592186514121} {:answer/id #uuid "e339479e-f7b9-56c7-8d79-9607ad1c038a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{cosh}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186514128}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186514121} :answer-field/id #uuid "6159fd9b-5adf-5789-a137-567ebbd5c693" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186105406}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d2c0a118-2d4e-50b2-93bb-bfb098208306" :question/math-academy-id "q-95686" :question/problem "Find the derivative of $f(x)=4{sinh}^{3}⁡x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=4{g}^{3},\,g=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=12{g}^{2}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =12{g}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cosh}⁡x \\  & =12{sinh}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186107022 :tutorial/content "The area bounded by a polar curve $r = r(\theta)$ and the rays $\theta = \theta_1$ and $\theta = \theta_2$ is given by

$$
\dfrac 1 2\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2\,\textrm d \theta \, .
$$

Calculating the integral is often straightforward if we know the integration limits $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. But what if we don't know these values?

For example, suppose we want to calculate the total area of the first petal of the curve $r=\sin(3\theta),$ shown below.

![](images/e0/e0c9059613162af33791e7edb7413dfbac9739cf24eeabd01b0033acba2b772a.png)

The curve bounding the blue petal crosses itself at the origin. When it passes through the origin, we must have $r=0,$ and since $r=\sin(3\theta),$ we have

$$
\sin(3\theta)=0 \, .
$$

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta \in [0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
3\theta = 0,\pi \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = 0, \theta_2 = \dfrac\pi 3,$ and the area of the first petal is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "774c3094-f23a-5a9b-90f7-90e89c6b5883" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1130 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186107119 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

Since the hyperbolic functions are defined in terms of exponential functions, we can easily calculate their derivatives. 

The derivatives of the basic hyperbolic functions are as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x) & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡x) & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) & ={sech}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use these results to find the derivative of the following function:

$$
y = \sinh{x} - 2\cosh{x}
$$

Using the usual properties of derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x-2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2\operatorname{cosh}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡x-2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "df316238-1ead-50db-80ec-d47656e6acad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5207 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186107120 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
%$

We would like the prove the following result:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\sinh{x}) = \cosh x
$$

To do this, we revert to the definition of the hyperbolic sine:

$$
\sinh x = \dfrac{1}{2}(e^x-e^{-x}).
$$

Differentiating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}) \\  & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

The proof for the derivative of the hyperbolic cosine is very similar. You may wish to try it for yourself." :tutorial/id #uuid "11e38932-d6a4-5649-bbbe-205fb1bad98d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5221 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Derivative of the Hyperbolic Sine"} {:db/id 17592186107121 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

We would like the prove the following result:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(\tanh{x}) = \sech^2{x}
$$

We do this using the definition of the hyperbolic tangent. The most convenient definition to work with for this purpose is

$$
\tanh{x} = \dfrac{e^{2x}-1}{e^{2x}+1}.
$$

Differentiating the above equation with respect to $x$ using the quotient rule, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{e}^{2x}-1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\right) \\  & =\frac{({e}^{2x}-1)^{′}\cdot ({e}^{2x}+1)-({e}^{2x}-1)\cdot ({e}^{2x}+1)^{′}}{({e}^{2x}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2{e}^{2x})({e}^{2x}+1)-({e}^{2x}-1)(2{e}^{2x})}{({e}^{2x}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{4x}+2{e}^{2x}-2{e}^{4x}+2{e}^{2x}}{({e}^{2x}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2x}}{({e}^{2x}+1)^{2}} \\  & ={\left(\frac{2{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\right)}^{2} \\  & ={\left(\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}\right)}^{2} \\  & ={sech}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2a7389d5-4ba5-5fd7-8edb-b983483e6099" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5223 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Derivative of the Hyperbolic Tangent"} {:db/id 17592186107155 :tutorial/content "Given a linear transformation $\mathbf T$ with an associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ there are three possibilities regarding the type of object formed under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ by a two-dimensional preimage. 

To demonstrate, consider the three-sided polygon $\mathcal P$ with vertices $(0,1)$, $(2,0)$ and $(2,1),$ as shown below. 

![](images/97/97689c7aaf7f6d42314fd01cb36b557df8081880659bcea08905e6c57f358ac1.png)

Let's describe the three possible types of object formed by the image of $\mathcal P{:}$

- Case where $T$ is non-singular:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:

<div class="matrix-operands matrix-operands-stacked">
<div>$T =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$</div>
</div>

We can easily check that $T$ is non-singular by computing its determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $\mathcal P$ and then compute the product $TX{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a triangle.

![](images/14/145753e4f69dfa67bb45f59b7e9ed8bca789c589d4c5340ce2112363fa70cd7b.png)

- Case where $\mathbf{T}$ is singular and has at least one nonzero entry:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:

$$
T = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

We can easily check that $T$ is singular by computing its determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 3-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 4 & 10 \\ 3 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of  $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

![](images/46/46d387dbf6678d324135dbbb3439688c0bdbf9f9567baef56f34aa4aa9ee22e3.png)

- Case where $T$ is the zero matrix:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation represented by the zero matrix:

$$
T = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Clearly, $T$ is singular. Now, computing the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are all $(0,0)$, the origin $O$ of the coordinate system. 

![](images/db/dbb9fce92da1f231a31e110f6cabb6faaf1bb43961a6c1de012c7c302c7af928.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "0bc95d9b-74ad-509c-8c28-e4e34606b376" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7702 :tutorial/title "Image Types Formed by Linear Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186110287 :question/id #uuid "3d64bc1e-3937-5e0d-b0f8-7dd06acd27ef" :question/math-academy-id "e-10052" :question/problem "Express $2\tan x\cdot(\cot x+\tan{x})$ in terms of $\sec x$ only." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+\tan^2 x = \sec^2{x}
$$

Also, recall the following identity:

$$
\cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tan x\cdot \cot x = 1
$$

Using the above identities, we can simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+2{tan}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2\cdot 1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2\text{ }\,(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =2\,{sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
2\tan x\cdot(\cot x+\tan{x})= 2\sec^2x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110288 :question/id #uuid "c04610a2-f73f-57a9-b17b-da9b30a5e431" :question/math-academy-id "e-10053" :question/problem "Express $(1-\sec x )(1+\sec x )$ in terms of $\tan x$ only." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+\tan^2 x = \sec^2{x}
$$

First, we expand the parentheses using the difference of squares formula:

$$
(1-\sec x )(1+\sec x ) = 1 - \sec^2x
$$

Then, we rewrite the expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{sec}^{2}⁡x & =1-(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =1-1-{tan}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-{tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(1-\sec x )(1+\sec x )= -\tan^2 x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110442 :question/id #uuid "b34736aa-e682-5ab3-85a0-dd86f49759f1" :question/math-academy-id "e-3143" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $\dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{1+\tan^2 \theta}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+\tan^2 \theta = \sec^2{\theta}
$$

We rewrite the given expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{\color{blue}1+\tan^2 \theta} = \dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{\color{blue}\sec^2 \theta}
$$

We now cancel the common factor of $\sec^2 \theta$ in the numerator and denominator and simplify the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{2\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }}{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{1+\tan^2 \theta} = 2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110453 :question/id #uuid "eceb2f88-2948-5037-bdbb-60483b3a2f34" :question/math-academy-id "e-3470" :question/problem "Simplify the trigonometric expression $\sin \theta \, (1 + \cot^2 \theta)$." :question/worked-solution "First, using the identity $1 + \cot^2 \theta = \csc^2 \theta,$ we rewrite the expression in the parentheses: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,(1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {csc}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the fact that $\csc {\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin{\theta}},$ we can further simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {csc}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110454 :question/id #uuid "0d77018a-b39f-57f6-b2b8-646c1ed73b9e" :question/math-academy-id "e-3472" :question/problem "Simplify $\dfrac{1}{\csc \theta - \cot \theta}.$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can simplify this expression by transforming the denominator into a form where we can apply a known trigonometric identity.

First, we multiply the numerator and the denominator of our expression by $\csc \theta + \cot \theta.$ This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta } & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta -{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\csc^2 \theta - \cot^2 \theta=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta -{cot}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{1} \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110455 :question/id #uuid "e3b17108-28ce-5a36-b211-05e6671c1f37" :question/math-academy-id "e-3473" :question/problem "Simplify $\csc x  + \csc x \cot^2 x  -\csc^3x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor $\csc x$ from the first two terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x{cot}^{2}⁡x-{csc}^{3}⁡x & =\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)-{csc}^{3}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the cotangent-cosecant identity,

$$
1+ \cot^2 x=\csc^2 x ,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)-{csc}^{3}⁡x & =\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot ({csc}^{2}⁡x)-{csc}^{3}⁡x \\  & ={csc}^{3}⁡x-{csc}^{3}⁡x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110457 :question/id #uuid "02c747c2-0eda-5c53-8e43-829f878dd278" :question/math-academy-id "e-3482" :question/problem "![](images/aa/aad0b38f5afb88c13039ac577a927e232d84905de40297ed824c966795ce7bb4.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{2}{3},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta.$" :question/worked-solution "Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

We're given that $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{5}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. 

So our final answer is $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 5}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186110458 :question/id #uuid "bbf71023-510c-54af-9d0c-4df6744e3007" :question/math-academy-id "e-3484" :question/problem "![](images/e5/e50848432dd18a4a5dc64d4e5a5cfb8b3e14e9fed6231774dd83ead5552cd463.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{2\sqrt 6}{7},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\csc\theta.$" :question/worked-solution "Again, any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

We're given that $x=\dfrac{2\sqrt 6}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{2\sqrt 6}{7}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{2\sqrt 6}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{24}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{5}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have

$$
\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)} = \dfrac{7}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110459 :question/id #uuid "ba6cc6a0-dbb8-58d2-9d02-c76310028d4e" :question/math-academy-id "e-3485" :question/problem "![](images/e6/e666ddc8a8eda452abd833e963446c96de5d34dfbf76e9c92564e85a48080524.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{4}{5},$ what is $\tan\theta?$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that $x=\dfrac{4}{5}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. Therefore $\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}.$

Using the fact that

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},
$$

we finally get

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)} = \dfrac {3}{4}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110460 :question/id #uuid "4da93c71-9a1e-512e-9735-14d7c6221378" :question/math-academy-id "e-3497" :question/problem "Simplify $\dfrac{1}{\csc \theta + \cot \theta} + \cot \theta.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the following identity: 

$$
1= \csc^2{\theta} -\cot^2{\theta}
$$

Substituting the above identity into the given expression, and then factoring it as a difference of squares, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }+\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta -{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }+\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )\,(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }+\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )\,\cancel{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}}{\cancel{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }}+\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\  & =(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )+\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110486 :question/id #uuid "4e63488a-97a0-5b21-ac91-2f0c9a1efa54" :question/math-academy-id "e-4014" :question/problem "Express $\log_3(2)+\log_3(5)$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡2+{log}_{3}⁡5 & ={log}_{3}⁡(2\cdot 5) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡10.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110487 :question/id #uuid "07d810ce-010c-5a07-8174-f01d9b807a60" :question/math-academy-id "e-4015" :question/problem "Express $3\log_{5}{7}+3\log_{5}{3}$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{log}_{5}⁡7+3{log}_{5}⁡3 & =3({log}_{5}⁡7+{log}_{5}⁡3) \\  & =3{log}_{5}⁡(7\cdot 3) \\  & =3{log}_{5}⁡21.\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$
3\log_{5}{7}+3\log_{5}{3} = 3\log_{5} 21 .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110489 :question/id #uuid "39a1c600-8d35-5671-bcb1-62682d750cd3" :question/math-academy-id "e-4018" :question/problem "If $\log_2(3)=k$ and $\log_2(x)=p,$ what is the value of $\log_2(3x)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$

Using the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(3x) & ={log}_{2}⁡3+{log}_{2}⁡x \\  & =k+p.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110490 :question/id #uuid "85379129-7b9e-507f-b70a-841c868cfa15" :question/math-academy-id "e-4020" :question/problem "Express $\log_3\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$ as a difference of logarithms." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the quotient rule for logarithms:

$$

$$

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) & ={log}_{3}⁡(2)-{log}_{3}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110491 :question/id #uuid "8a8c6256-216f-5516-ac07-80311c557f4b" :question/math-academy-id "e-4022" :question/problem "Write $\log_5(16) - \log_5(8)$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the quotient rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n(a) - \log_n(b) = \log_n\left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right)
$$

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡(16)-{log}_{5}⁡(8) & ={log}_{5}⁡\left(\frac{16}{8}\right) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110492 :question/id #uuid "23ccceb8-73ee-58c7-9787-ae1eb6b3f53f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4023" :question/problem "Express $2\log_2(25) - 2\log_2(5)$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the quotient rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n(a) - \log_n(b) = \log_n\left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the quotient rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{log}_{2}⁡(25)-2{log}_{2}⁡(5) & =2({log}_{2}⁡(25)-{log}_{2}⁡(5)) \\  & =2({log}_{2}⁡\left(\frac{25}{5}\right)) \\  & =2{log}_{2}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
2\log_2(25) - 2\log_2(5) = 2\log_2(5).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110494 :question/id #uuid "7c937587-dc81-5ee9-aa66-a509a87433e2" :question/math-academy-id "e-4067" :question/problem "Find the exact solution of the equation $2^{x+1}=3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we take $\log_2$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{x+1} & =3 \\ {log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x+1}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x+1 = \log_2 \left( 3 \right).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ x & ={log}_{2}⁡(3)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x= \log_2 \left( 3 \right) - 1.$"} {:db/id 17592186110498 :question/id #uuid "53a33ca5-8a37-5ec7-acb2-00e3471a1c6a" :question/math-academy-id "e-4079" :question/problem "By expressing $\dfrac{1}{2}\log_3{x}$ in the form $\log_3 \left(x^k\right),$ determine the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n(c^m)= m\log_n\left( c \right)
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{log}_{3}⁡x & ={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k = \dfrac{1}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186110502 :question/id #uuid "c6d0d3ad-111a-5db1-b521-0c9416dfb6b8" :question/math-academy-id "e-4140" :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) = 2\log_4(3x)-1?$" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2{log}_{4}⁡(3x)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{log}_{4}⁡(3y)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{log}_{4}⁡(3y)-1 \\ 2{log}_{4}⁡(3y) & =x+1 \\ {log}_{4}⁡(3y) & =\frac{x+1}{2} \\ {4}^{{log}_{4}⁡(3y)} & ={4}^{(x+1)/2} \\ 3y & ={4}^{(x+1)/2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}{4}^{(x+1)/2}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) =\dfrac13 4^{(x+1)/2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186110899 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04345df0-7962-5e87-a668-8e2fee2a965f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186250584} {:answer/id #uuid "3aee499c-0172-5b4d-89b9-dee7dcf4cd89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta -1" :db/id 17592186251043} {:answer/id #uuid "a240eee2-5ae9-586b-b764-5e820161af72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186251952} {:answer/id #uuid "b98848f4-b478-5189-bd30-49aaeff065a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186252185} {:answer/id #uuid "e5bb6155-781c-5ef1-a08d-fc42d17e5eda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186252564}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186252564} :answer-field/id #uuid "097ffcf1-4dde-5aa6-9350-1d25c27efe0f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186252825}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b383bf3c-484a-57e7-86ef-8a613fbe3df4" :question/math-academy-id "q-119914" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta -{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta -{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110900 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "221a4245-8d36-54ef-a82d-e80ee76d86ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\sqrt{6}}{2}" :db/id 17592186257060} {:answer/id #uuid "77312d37-9886-5569-95f9-c48a271a75f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt{6}}{9}" :db/id 17592186257837} {:answer/id #uuid "8319e688-c42a-58a8-aa2e-6c419db98208" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}" :db/id 17592186257942} {:answer/id #uuid "aa4aecba-9357-5bb7-978f-a673979c6b60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt{6}}{12}" :db/id 17592186258268} {:answer/id #uuid "b24f29ad-ae26-5c1a-98cc-8488a4660ab6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{12}" :db/id 17592186258335}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258268} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ed6599f-2974-5160-b981-962e1c285d91" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2755d3ad-f502-5322-8d2b-3addfcafe3f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-124750" :question/problem "![](images/bd/bd8650a856fe3136759d81a886b2d4622cf3eb463b75e6023b44083c72f63a1a.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{1}{5},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $sec⁡\theta .$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/73/734eef45985ddfb6450666e1dd32c6d3beab9ca3aef66c87c6ba393d6960b08b.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{1}{5}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{5}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}.$

Knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}\right)}=\frac{5}{2\sqrt{6}}.
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡\theta  & =\frac{5}{2\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2\sqrt{6}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{6}}{2\cdot 6} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{6}}{12}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110985 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d3dc6496-77c0-520f-b529-b7f00becd583" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4^{\frac{x}{5}}+1}{10}" :db/id 17592186537646}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186537646} :answer-field/id #uuid "d7396d89-4bc9-5ba9-b9b1-12012d5351ed" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186107628}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9ae8277e-37c6-59e9-af56-0d7eccfa6c61" :question/math-academy-id "q-228842" :question/problem "The inverse of the function $f(x)=5{log}_{4}⁡(10x-1)$ is ${f}^{-1}(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5{log}_{4}⁡(10x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{log}_{4}⁡(10y-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{log}_{4}⁡(10y-1) \\ {log}_{4}⁡(10y-1) & =\frac{x}{5} \\ {4}^{{log}_{4}⁡(10y-1)} & ={4}^{x/5} \\ 10y-1 & ={4}^{x/5} \\ 10y & ={4}^{x/5}+1 \\ y & =\frac{{4}^{x/5}+1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{{4}^{x/5}+1}{10}.$"} {:db/id 17592186110994 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "108b997f-3ef8-51bd-8557-0ff04c25f1bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{cos}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186288157} {:answer/id #uuid "7041b720-f438-5081-b848-05a44b0aed85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186288814} {:answer/id #uuid "78afce16-dd3c-5a3e-ac4b-6998edd1f35d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186288862} {:answer/id #uuid "f3b3fb44-66d6-5d64-93da-9ca291156c95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186289642} {:answer/id #uuid "fb5e503b-835c-559e-adc2-29bda28d6008" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186289689}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186288814} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f020196-633d-58ab-b488-e011bb361efe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186289936}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e2a7de17-dd0e-54fa-9258-ee9fa753362a" :question/math-academy-id "q-23602" :question/problem "Simplify $$
\displaystyle \frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ we rewrite and simplify the expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta }{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110995 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7f882725-62cc-5898-8d2e-ff3635b7245e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186288895} {:answer/id #uuid "83fb364b-83af-5109-8ea3-680bb950ca7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186288919} {:answer/id #uuid "859697f6-521a-5fca-b453-f2892d6773ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186288935} {:answer/id #uuid "c8a6fee2-b4d2-5e71-b1ad-677ad6dc68d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +1" :db/id 17592186289361} {:answer/id #uuid "ebeac752-db32-5a50-9ca3-c078af79f75b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186289592}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186288895} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a2a6126-cf07-5c07-bd8b-97a45a84e6d8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186289921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7a901438-c891-5987-9100-1b001a426058" :question/math-academy-id "q-23638" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We rewrite the given expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }=\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }
$$

We now simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }}{\cancel{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following identities:

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

 

Using the above identities, we can further simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta } & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111031 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15010333-4fe3-58c3-9b8d-774f22c98a0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{125}⁡48" :db/id 17592186539520} {:answer/id #uuid "34191607-a84f-520a-941b-c61abefe22a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{5}⁡10" :db/id 17592186539576} {:answer/id #uuid "44f711d5-f916-58a0-9fd2-f9692427848c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{15}⁡48" :db/id 17592186539607} {:answer/id #uuid "566a2d36-e8a0-5180-945f-a8d73a39229d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{15}⁡12" :db/id 17592186539627} {:answer/id #uuid "8d50a5b0-9844-5e2c-97e0-9c0453654ffa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{5}⁡48" :db/id 17592186539718}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539718} :answer-field/id #uuid "1dc7909b-ed18-5a26-b360-ce0bd7c2f4b2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186107941}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9cb9b8d4-254b-58ff-bc4a-531da47e017a" :question/math-academy-id "q-24424" :question/problem "Express ${log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(2\cdot 4)+{log}_{5}⁡6 \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(8\cdot 6) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡48.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111055 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "027931f1-c81a-5437-9a6a-eaecb93a762a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{3}+x)" :db/id 17592186542646} {:answer/id #uuid "586a7d70-5172-59a1-9741-2c4ca73c06b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{2}⁡(x)" :db/id 17592186542882} {:answer/id #uuid "87cfe6cf-ae32-54c0-8cf9-e7edf787bdc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{3}-x)" :db/id 17592186542999} {:answer/id #uuid "af492c68-51a5-5572-bb8d-b7ffebbda341" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{3})" :db/id 17592186543096} {:answer/id #uuid "d83c88c8-1213-5064-9f38-c3cdba0753f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2})" :db/id 17592186543193}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186543193} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e31e373-15da-5c90-abf8-352f69c53e7c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186108087}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1ffe9f61-1ba3-54d9-b9af-4cad3fb8f150" :question/math-academy-id "q-25233" :question/problem "Express ${log}_{2}⁡({x}^{3})-{log}_{2}⁡(x)$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the quotient rule for logarithms:

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as:
