Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{bmatrix},
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-3-\lambda  & 2 \\ -5 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +13 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=-2\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+3\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+3\text{i}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1-3\text{i} & 2 \\ -5 & 1-3\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}1-3\text{i} \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129683 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "47e55c69-1866-588d-872a-b402386f3e06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186368516} {:answer/id #uuid "aaf80517-57f1-595e-a0c6-e931586cc9b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186368517} {:answer/id #uuid "d3509644-e4ea-51d2-a471-d35c123da88d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186368518} {:answer/id #uuid "00e54f49-e547-573b-a5d0-5831fa66ad14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186368519} {:answer/id #uuid "6e481d77-a41c-5160-be87-d2c659c36170" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186368520}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368519} :answer-field/id #uuid "38d5c140-2980-57f5-9c02-49b92c04d215" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186368515}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "58dcf2b4-e0ab-52d4-9f82-d78c5ef8a397" :question/math-academy-id "q-38655" :question/problem "$$

$$
B=\left[\begin{array}{c|cc}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & \text{Re}({\lambda }_{2}) & \text{Im}({\lambda }_{2}) \\ 0 & -\text{Im}({\lambda }_{2}) & \text{Re}({\lambda }_{2})\end{array}\right],\,\,P=\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ {v}_{1} & \text{Re}({v}_{2}) & \text{Im}({v}_{2}) \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}.

Swapping the blocks on the main diagonal of $B$ will result in switching the corresponding columns in $P.$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 3-\lambda  & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1(-1)) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the real eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{2,3} & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-4}}{2} \\  & =1\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $A$ is a rotation-scaling matrix. So, we need to find its scale factor and the angle of rotation.

We can find the scale factor using the following formula:

$$

Now, we can represent $A$ as a product of a rotation and a scaling matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}r & 0 \\ 0 & r\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

Hence, we obtain that

$$

Therefore, in order to find $Av$, we need to rotate $v$ counterclockwise by an angle of $\frac{\pi }{4}$  and scale the result by a scale factor of $2,$ as shown below.

You may assume that $\theta $ is a fixed constant." :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129758 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0cf20c60-05f2-5708-980b-fd1527c75409" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int "![](images/22/2206a1bc02acb9ddccc5991a4c8d36c9e5d3255e72239e8f7e81908e10faab48.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=18y$ for $x\ge 0$ and $z\ge 0,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}xy\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at $(0,3,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=18y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =18y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =18\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -18\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =18\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/57/578c7f81a0dae8339772dec9a9407fb380866e5dde5fdd18fee04feb6afe5749.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 18\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

$$

$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =4\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2},$ what is the value of $tan⁡\theta ?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/94/948610f67267e6ec1b845d2b4e1bc4030b81a1080bcb9a44d9f974ff78c3f7b0.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Finally, knowing that $tan⁡\theta =\frac{sin⁡\theta }{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
tan⁡\theta =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129832 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8310669b-d2b3-547a-ba25-e02eadad68f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{25}" "![](images/fd/fd1a5a140c3a2d430312d6f6ceeb21d6b7282119c8ec53365553ff845d8c64d5.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,
$$ where the region $D$ is the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at 
$(0,-\frac{1}{2}).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{-{y}^{2}-y}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{-{y}^{2}-y} \\ {x}^{2} & =-{y}^{2}-y \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ((-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{sin}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({sin}^{5}⁡0-{sin}^{5}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186130323 :tutorial/content "We've seen that we can write a rotation-scaling matrix $A$ is the product of a rotation and a scaling matrix:

$$
A
	= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}r & 0 \\ 0 & r\end{array} \right]}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\cos   \theta  & - \sin   \theta  \\ \sin   \theta  & \cos   \theta \end{array} \right]}
$$

So, the natural question now is, how does a rotation-scaling matrix 
$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}a} & - {\color{red}b} \\ {\color{red}b} & {\color{blue}a}\end{array} \right]}
$$
relate to the individual rotation and scaling matrices?

First, setting the two equal to each other, we get

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}a} & - {\color{red}b} \\ {\color{red}b} & {\color{blue}a}\end{array} \right]}
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}r & 0 \\ 0 & r\end{array} \right]}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\cos   \theta  & - \sin   \theta  \\ \sin   \theta  & \cos   \theta \end{array} \right]}.
$$

From this, we can find the scale factor and angle of rotation of a rotation-scaling matrix. First, notice that we have

$$
{\color{blue}a} = {\color{blue}r\cos\theta}, \quad \textrm{and}\quad {\color{red}b} = {\color{red}r\sin\theta}.
$$

To find $r$ in terms of $a$ and $b,$ we can square and then add the two equations above. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the scale factor $r$ is given by

$$
r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} = \sqrt{\det{A}}.
$$

Similarly, to find the rotation angle $\theta$ in terms of $a$ and $b,$ we start with the equations

$$
{\color{blue}a} = {\color{blue}r\cos\theta}, \quad \textrm{and}\quad {\color{red}b} = {\color{red}r\sin\theta}.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{b}{a}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta = \arctan\left(\dfrac ba \right).
$$

It's also possible to recover both the original scaling *and* rotation matrix once the scale factor $r$ is known. Let's see how that works." :tutorial/id #uuid "1fb2c1d9-0856-55ca-945a-8e01f2e58902" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2014 :tutorial/title "Finding the Scale Factor and Rotation Angle Of a Rotation-Scaling Matrix"} {:db/id 17592186130333 :tutorial/content "By the Pythagorean theorem, we know that the equation 

$$
x^2+y^2 = 1
$$

holds for any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle. 

Now, we also know that for any point on the unit circle, the coordinates $(x,y)$ are related to the central angle $\theta$ via the formulas

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

Substituting the above into the Pythagorean Identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The last equation is called the **Pythagorean trigonometric identity**, and it holds for *every* angle $\theta.$ This includes negative angles and angles that are larger than one full rotation." :tutorial/id #uuid "2adb34b1-9f8d-5f02-bafd-029ac9251084" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2721 :tutorial/title "The Pythagorean Identity"} {:db/id 17592186130444 :tutorial/content "Rational expressions are *closed* under the arithmetic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

So, we have that:

- The *sum* of two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} + \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
- The *difference* between two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} - \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
- The *product* of two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} \:\cdot\: \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
- The *quotient* of two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} \div \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
provided that the denominator is nonzero.

In this sense, rational expressions and rational numbers have similar properties." :tutorial/id #uuid "0e3a486b-3804-5128-a6b4-9865034f8c9b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6059 :tutorial/title "Closure Properties of Rational Expressions"} {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array} \right]} = \mathbf{T}\left( {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v \\ w\end{array} \right]} \right) = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \sin   v \cos   w \\ u \sin   v \sin   w \\ u \cos   v\end{array} \right]}
$$ 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

$$
\mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v \\ w\end{array} \right]} 
\longrightarrow 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v , w ) \\ y ( u , v , w ) \\ z ( u , v , w )\end{array} \right]}
$$ 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\begin{vmatrix}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{vmatrix}+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

$$
\mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} 
\longrightarrow 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]}.
$$ 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} = \mathbf{T}\left( {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} \right) = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \cos   v \\ u \sin   v\end{array} \right]}
$$ 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} {:db/id 17592186130466 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}, \qquad
t \in [0,\pi].
$$

If we rotate this curve by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we obtain a sphere of radius $1.$ 

![](images/d0/d0d323b764b70d3f2830d821636a9bc27b40e7f7e9f45df909c81dd279dc16e4.png)

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of our surface of revolution can be computed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi (-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-2\pi (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-2\pi (-1-1) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f849fe7f-670f-5a7f-8dc7-dbbd33a876f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7707 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that 

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi,
$$

we first  calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\begin{vmatrix}-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\end{vmatrix}-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot (-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ))-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86bd6cae-b4e6-5da9-80b3-b884c320bda3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7720 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Jacobian for Spherical Polar Coordinates"} {:db/id 17592186130481 :tutorial/content "As we know already, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with zero and negative exponents. To demonstrate, let's compute the value of

$$
(-3)^0 +2^2 \div 2.
$$

To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Notice that $\left(-3\right)^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-3)}^{0}+{2}^{2}÷2 &= 1+{2}^{2}÷2 \\ &= 1+4÷2 \\ &= 1+2 \\ &= 3.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e2d29fa0-8bcb-537b-bed9-91a9ff109764" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8061 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186133496 :question/id #uuid "fc3055a3-5118-5a5b-8150-caadbfdae02b" :question/math-academy-id "e-12788" :question/problem "What is the reciprocal of $-21?$" :question/worked-solution "To find the reciprocal of $-21,$ we divide $1$ by $-21.$ So, we obtain 

$$
1 \div (-21) = -\dfrac{1}{21}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186133712 :question/id #uuid "74c9ecfb-5005-53ff-b7a9-db798488587b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9554" :question/problem "Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 2\sin t, \: 2 \cos t \rangle$ for $t \in \left [0, 2\pi \right).$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D) 
= \iint\limits_D  \left(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} -  \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \mathrm{d}A
= \int_0^{2\pi} \boxed{ {\phantom{A A A A A A A}}}\: \mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*

![](images/a5/a5eeb5db90f9ee0d86a49e5bbf02629c7886fa019db7cff3c4d0e1eb43e8fd75.png)" :question/worked-solution "Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
- \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle  2\cos t ,\:  -2 \sin t \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $4\cos^2 t.$"} {:db/id 17592186134064 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00a97740-bf4e-5245-a223-1105ad76868c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238086} {:answer/id #uuid "0ccb496a-1f3e-5f9c-9be5-7756bb97a385" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238169} {:answer/id #uuid "9dbfd16e-b04d-5762-91cf-d69f6af7923d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239432} {:answer/id #uuid "a5578604-9539-5565-8bbb-579ff2d23c8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239490} {:answer/id #uuid "ff74f82e-113d-5ba7-9d63-962e019ecfd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186240320}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238086} :answer-field/id #uuid "50e2f23b-8197-5ffd-805f-f3ecff761a73" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240475}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e7a8c44b-b300-5e66-9428-e03f400ebf5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-105416" :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134134 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00d95993-6fce-50a6-9da0-c38e0b9621ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186130961} {:answer/id #uuid "5b48ccdf-94f7-5b30-b9e9-c2b9d97a02fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186130965} {:answer/id #uuid "6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\pi " :db/id 17592186521016} {:answer/id #uuid "81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186521062} {:answer/id #uuid "9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186521119}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186521062} :answer-field/id #uuid "cfbd2886-ea55-5ec0-b21b-dda63331dd6e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186130960}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "008f670b-b77a-5939-9c4f-8602d138cc7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-162377" :question/problem "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-0\cdot \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134384 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07ce7e4c-f358-59e1-83ec-c12d185581ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186326996} {:answer/id #uuid "4c81f4db-d861-547d-a06f-42826d808a37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186327598} {:answer/id #uuid "ae66382d-5670-5d2c-88f6-a6e2c5123b49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186328448} {:answer/id #uuid "b25772cd-af85-5333-aa05-8ae7885a5e83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186328481} {:answer/id #uuid "b2a08351-6bdd-5434-861e-a5f6e60e14fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186328483}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186328448} :answer-field/id #uuid "033cf0fb-22d2-5315-bb5f-00c4ceeb328a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186329191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "663f08e4-70a8-54d4-a465-2c24f8e60288" :question/math-academy-id "q-42254" :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$ Find $⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We need to evaluate

$$
⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}]-[\frac{1}{3}(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134394 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4731d43a-1037-5467-97a5-e798a96ef9d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186327555} {:answer/id #uuid "658a8d30-d9af-5e26-83da-9719b1081d76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186327818} {:answer/id #uuid "6d1056e6-0216-54a8-a348-f7fd16cd261c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186327879} {:answer/id #uuid "cb4f71df-9ae0-539d-bc37-b9dfa1a2efd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186328715} {:answer/id #uuid "f61627d1-d9a7-5fa0-8601-a797fc2e5d46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186329093}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186329093} :answer-field/id #uuid "3ecac406-0aef-584c-9d48-0a6c47d439e8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186329307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a804e446-7433-50c7-a8ce-2769d7a93237" :question/math-academy-id "q-42459" :question/problem "Find $4det(A)+4det(B)$, where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2\sqrt{2} & 1 \\ 1 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & \sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each matrix in turn.

- For the matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det(A)=2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}-1\cdot 1=3.
$$

- Since $B$ has proportional columns, we obtain

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}1} & \sqrt{2} & {\color{blue}2} \\ {\color{blue}2} & 1 & {\color{blue}4} \\ {\color{blue}3} & 6 & {\color{blue}6}\end{bmatrix}\hspace{2em}⟹\hspace{2em}det(B)=0.
$$

Therefore, $4det(A)+4det(B)=4\cdot 3+4\cdot 0=12.$"} {:db/id 17592186134395 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c225eb90-e2e0-5316-bf2c-433fb3c69768" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186132410} {:answer/id #uuid "320e4a8c-eedf-5588-98e8-c145e0ace715" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186132411} {:answer/id #uuid "43de3423-2ffd-5930-9ee0-ea5001c9a16b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186132412} {:answer/id #uuid "53f34a5f-dc76-5b22-9b1f-04217732f9e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186132413} {:answer/id #uuid "796055cc-72c1-5b68-9805-3a39d9b06647" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186132414}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186132410} :answer-field/id #uuid "33879ed2-4ff8-5792-966a-daa49f7bc975" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186132409}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "dcb38d39-eeab-5f94-bc9b-9cb1d6df2c04" :question/math-academy-id "q-42461" :question/problem "Find $2det(A)+4det(B)$, where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \sqrt{3} & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & \sqrt{2} & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each matrix in turn.

- Since $A$ is a triangular matrix, its determinant is given by the product of the elements of the main diagonal: 

$$
det(A)=1\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 1=4
$$

- Since $B$ has two identical rows, we obtain

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & \sqrt{2} & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,det(B)=0.
$$

Therefore, $2det(A)+4det(B)=2\cdot 4+4\cdot 0=8.$"} {:db/id 17592186134403 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b168093-06ee-59d2-a609-623e2ec4e449" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\pi }" :db/id 17592186327451} {:answer/id #uuid "4588a6ee-dc15-5f53-86b2-b586c559c781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186327542} {:answer/id #uuid "4f67b91c-0f60-548d-8a33-48f8a99a74b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{3\pi }{2}}" :db/id 17592186327627} {:answer/id #uuid "59ccd062-fdab-5575-acd3-736c657f5624" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{\pi }" :db/id 17592186327721} {:answer/id #uuid "ebca9d1f-42e9-5b29-8145-61126df47e3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}" :db/id 17592186328998}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186328998} :answer-field/id #uuid "9fca567e-a930-5cf5-8fe9-bab4358653b6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186329451}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f27dcc08-cb74-544e-b846-2c5aa548a3f7" :question/math-academy-id "q-42734" :question/problem "Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\left(\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(\frac{2\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi }{4})-(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4}) \\  & =(\pi +0)-(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186135151 :tutorial/content "If an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

For example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:

$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{array} \right]}
$$

The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\ast$) may represent any number.

Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)^{2+1}({\color{red}0})\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+2}({\color{red}0})\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+3}({\color{red}0})\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0+0+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "cee0a552-60f2-5785-a506-63bd053364c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186135172 :tutorial/content "The **reciprocal** of a number is equal to ${\color{red}{1}}$ divided by the number. For example:

- the reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{2}}$ is equal to ${\color{red}{1}} \div {\color{blue}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

- the reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{3}}$ is equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \div {\color{blue}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

- the reciprocal of $-{\color{blue}{7}}$ is equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \div ({\color{blue}{-7}}) = -\dfrac{1}{7}$

The reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{1}}$ is  equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \div {\color{blue}{1}} = 1.$ So the number $1$ is equal to its reciprocal. The same is true for $-1.$

The reciprocal of a number always has the same sign as the original number.

- If the number is positive, its reciprocal will be positive, while

- if the number is negative, its reciprocal is also negative." :tutorial/id #uuid "bcbb31e1-711c-5521-b35a-8fe1e56f4b95" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8017 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "f6ba1c77-7947-50fa-9bf1-7b1374d40c43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{m}{min^{2}}" :db/id 17592186137556} {:answer/id #uuid "687385c3-7a8d-58d5-b147-ba9261548880" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{m^{2}}{min^{2}}" :db/id 17592186137558} {:answer/id #uuid "699eb470-cd2b-5ea6-8de7-eb6a87b032e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{m^{3}}{min^{3}}" :db/id 17592186137559} {:db/id 17592186138086 :question/id #uuid "c70c6338-9fcf-5672-a5f5-47ff0c8a2bf4" :question/math-academy-id "e-13470" :question/problem "Find the value of $2\,\dfrac 5 {10} + 4\,\dfrac 3 {10}$." :question/worked-solution "To add two mixed numbers, we add

- whole numbers to whole numbers, and
- fractions to fractions.

With that in mind let's add our mixed numbers.

- Adding the whole numbers, we get
$2 + 4 = {\color{red}{6}}$.
- Adding the fractions, we get
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac 5 {10} + \dfrac 3 {10} = \dfrac{5+3}{10} = \dfrac 8 {10}.
$$
We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $2{:}$
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{8}{10} = \dfrac{8\div 2}{10\div 2} = {\color{blue}{\dfrac{4}{5}}}
$$

Therefore,

$$
2\,\dfrac 5 {10} + 4\,\dfrac 3 {10} = {\color{red}{6}} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac 4 5}} = 6\,\dfrac 4 5
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138091 :question/id #uuid "be7e80d2-601c-5320-9aa0-f017331c5607" :question/math-academy-id "e-13500" :question/problem "Which mixed number is equivalent to $51.4$?" :question/worked-solution "Whenever we write a decimal as a mixed number, our mixed number will have

- a *whole number part* that corresponds to the whole number to the left of the decimal point, and
- a *fractional part* that corresponds to the decimal part to the right of the decimal point.

With that in mind, let's write ${\color{blue}51}.\!{\color{red}4}$ as a mixed number.

- The whole number part is ${\color{blue}51}$.
- The decimal part has $1$ decimal place, so we can write it as a fraction in the following way:
$0.4= \dfrac{4}{10}$
Now we reduce the fraction to its simplest form by dividing the numerator and denominator by $2{:}$
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{4 \div 2}{10 \div 2} = {\color{red}\dfrac{2}{5}}
$$

Therefore, we can write the given decimal as the following mixed number:

$$
51.4 = 51 \, \dfrac{2}{5}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138100 :question/id #uuid "105a0a49-ea48-51f8-961d-269ec910b94c" :question/math-academy-id "e-13550" :question/problem "What mixed number is equivalent to $\dfrac{71}{8}$?" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide $71$ by ${\color{blue}{8}}{:}$

$$
71 \div 8 = 8\, \textrm{R}\,{\color{red}{7}}
$$

So, our division gives $8$ wholes, and we're left with

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}7}{\color{blue}8}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{71}{8} = 8\,\dfrac{\color{red}7}{\color{blue}8}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138101 :question/id #uuid "3ba209c9-cae2-5c20-86f4-44c571c223f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-13551" :question/problem "Find a mixed number equivalent to $\dfrac{51}{6}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we divide $51$ by ${\color{blue}{6}}{:}$

$$
51 \div 6 = 8 \, \textrm{R}\, {\color{red}{3}}
$$

So, our division gives $8$ wholes, and we're left with

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}6}
$$

We can reduce the fraction

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}6}
$$

to its lowest terms by dividing the numerator and denominator by $3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{6} &= \frac{3 \div 3}{6 \div 3} = \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our mixed number is equivalent to

$$
8 \,\dfrac{1}{2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138118 :question/id #uuid "a5996998-a210-5da2-8b86-b3bf579d134a" :question/math-academy-id "e-13622" :question/problem "Which fraction is equivalent to $0.05$?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $0.05$ has $2$ decimal places. So, we can write it as a fraction with $100$ in the denominator:

$$
0.05 = \dfrac{5}{100}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its simplest form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{5}{100} &= \frac{5 \div 5}{100 \div 5} \\
&= \frac{1}{100 \div 5} \\
&= \frac{1}{10 \cdot 10 \div 5} \\
&= (1)/(10 \cdot (10 \div 5)) \\
&= \frac{1}{10 \cdot 2} \\
&= \frac{1}{20}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $0.05$ is equivalent to

$$
\dfrac{1}{20}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138120 :question/id #uuid "7d309af0-bf42-570a-bc5a-9dc01ca974d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13636" :question/problem "What is the value of $\dfrac 3 8 + \dfrac 1 8$?" :question/worked-solution "To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore,

$$
\frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3 + 1}{8} = \frac{4}{8}
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and the denominator by $4{:}$

$$
\dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{4\div 4}{8\div 4} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac 3 8 + \dfrac 1 8 = \dfrac 1 2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138121 :question/id #uuid "f2d34ef1-81be-5999-9df2-9165bef2c53c" :question/math-academy-id "e-13637" :question/problem "Find the value of $\dfrac 2 3 + \dfrac 2 3$." :question/worked-solution "To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same. $$

$$

We then convert

$$
\dfrac 4 3
$$

to a mixed number:

$$
4\div 3 = 1\,\textrm{R}1 = 1\,\dfrac 1 3
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac 2 3 + \dfrac 2 3 = 1\,\dfrac 1 3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138122 :question/id #uuid "44ca0914-a69b-5081-bc5a-7d8dd2af01b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-13679" :question/problem "What is the value of $5\,\dfrac{1}{2} + 2\,\dfrac 1 6$?" :question/worked-solution "To add two mixed numbers, we add whole numbers to whole numbers and fractions to fractions.

**Step 1**: Adding the whole numbers, we get

$$
5+2 = {\color{red}{7}}
$$

**Step 2**: Now we add the fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac 1 6
$$

To add two fractions with unlike denominators, we must express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

Here, we can make a common denominator of $6$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a denominator of $6$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $3$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1\times 3}{2\times 3} = \dfrac{3}{6}
$$

We can now add the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we add the numerators.

$$
\frac{3}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{6}
$$

Notice that we can simplify the above fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{4\div 2}{6\div 2} = \color{blue} \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

**Step 3**: Combining our results gives:

$$
{\color{red}{7}} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac 2 3}} = 7\,\dfrac 2 3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138124 :question/id #uuid "0bf56bec-fdab-5094-8d26-0b57e7522eb8" :question/math-academy-id "e-13682" :question/problem "Find the value of $1\,\dfrac{1}{2} + 3\,\dfrac 3 4$." :question/worked-solution "To add two mixed numbers, we add whole numbers to whole numbers and fractions to fractions.

**Step 1**: Adding the whole numbers, we get

$$
1+3 = {\color{red}{4}}
$$

**Step 2**: Now we add the fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac 3 4
$$

To add two fractions with unlike denominators, we must express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $4$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a denominator of $4$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1\times 2}{2\times 2} = \dfrac{2}{4}
$$

We can now add the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we add the numerators.

$$
\frac{2}{4} + \frac{3}{4} = \frac{5}{4}
$$

Notice that this is an improper fraction. We can convert the fraction

$$
\dfrac{5}{4}
$$

to a mixed number in the usual way:

$$
5\div 4 = 1\,\textrm{R}1 = {\color{blue}{1\,\dfrac 1{4}}}
$$

**Step 3**: We combine the results to get our answer.

$$
{\color{red}{4}} + {\color{blue}{1\,\dfrac 1{4}}} = 5\,\dfrac 1{4}
$$

Notice that we needed to add the whole numbers one final time."} {:db/id 17592186138125 :question/id #uuid "f39c2dd0-f416-5bc4-b282-a732408716da" :question/math-academy-id "e-13686" :question/problem "Find the value of $\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac 1 6$." :question/worked-solution "To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we must express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

Since $\color{blue}6$ is a multiple of ${\color{red}{3}}$, we can make a common denominator of ${\color{blue}{6}}$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 2 {\color{red}{3}}
$$

over a denominator of ${\color{blue}{6}}$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\dfrac{2}{\color{red}3} = \dfrac{2\times 2}{{\color{red}{3}}\times 2} = \dfrac{4}{\color{blue}6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators.

$$
\frac{4}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{3}{6}
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $3$:

$$
\dfrac{3\div 3}{6\div 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138139 :question/id #uuid "8f412bc3-e3fb-56da-8ded-e201ca5086c5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13767" :question/problem "Evaluate $6\,\dfrac{1}{2} - 3\,\dfrac 3 {10}$." :question/worked-solution "To subtract two mixed numbers, we subtract whole numbers from whole numbers and fractions from fractions.

**Step 1**: Subtracting the whole numbers, we get

$$
6-3 = {\color{red}{3}}
$$

**Step 2**: Now we subtract the fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac 3 {10}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this example, we can make a common denominator of $10$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a denominator of $10$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $5$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1\times 5}{2\times 5} = \dfrac{5}{10}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators.

$$
\frac{5}{10} - \frac{3}{10} = \frac{2}{10}
$$

Next, we reduce the fraction to its lowest terms.

$$
\dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{2\div 2}{10\div 2} = \color{blue} \dfrac{1}{5}
$$

**Step 3**: We combine the results to get our final answer:

$$
{\color{red}3} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac 1 5}} = {\color{red}{3}}\,{\color{blue}{\dfrac 1 5}}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138155 :question/id #uuid "135fa171-6d8d-508b-96b9-edca29e2aa54" :question/math-academy-id "e-13889" :question/problem "Calculate $256 \div 10$." :question/worked-solution "First, we write down our number. $$

$$

:question/problem "What is $0.7 \div 10$?"} {:db/id 17592186139623 :tutorial/content "We can use place value charts to divide decimals by $10$. For instance, to find the value of

$$
28 \div 10
$$

we perform the following steps.

**Step 1.** Write down the place value chart for $28$:



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">

<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>

<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>

<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
</tr>

**Step 2.** Move all digits by one place to the *right.*



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>

<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$8$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


Therefore,

$$
28\div 10 = 2.8 \,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6efc441f-c349-5538-bbf8-fc748aa7ddbd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1951 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186139624 :tutorial/content "When dividing by a power of ten, we shift the digits in the place value chart to the *right* by the number of zeros in the power of ten.

To illustrate, let's find the value of $47.2 \div 100$.

**Step 1.** Write down the place value chart for $47.2$:



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>hundredths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>thousandths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center">$4$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$7$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


**Step 2.** Determine the number of places to move. We're dividing by $100$, which has $\color{blue}2$ zeros, so we move all values to the *right* by $\color{blue}2$ places:



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>hundredths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>thousandths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$4$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$7$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


**Step 3.** Put zero in all empty cells that are to the right of the decimal point. We can also put a zero in the ones place if it is empty.



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
